scope: Mechanical inventory; original fields retained verbatim. Reviewer findings and judgments are advisory, not adjudicated facts. Keeps and claim journeys included.

locator.quote: We give the complete argument with explicit constants

entry.feedback: The opening promises a complete argument, but §1.3 later exempts the Forrelation supplier, parts of the construction, standard amplification, and several refinements proved only in the record. A specialist cannot tell from the abstract which result is actually proved in this document and which is supplied as a lemma.
entry.why_it_matters: The reader starts auditing a self-contained paper and only later learns its intended dependency boundary.
entry.advice: Describe the companion as proving the separation from stated ingredients, and distinguish the detailed reconstruction in the record. Keep the exceptions in one short, clearly labelled dependency paragraph; do not add review-status disclaimers.

locator.quote: comparisons need to be reliable only for the winner

entry.feedback: This is the most useful sentence in the abstract. It singles out the precise obstacle that prevents a routine reduction to an ordinary comparison problem.
entry.why_it_matters: A quantum-algorithms reader can immediately identify the hypothesis that makes the new tournament worth inspecting.
entry.advice: Protect this sentence through cuts, and make it the organising claim of the quantum overview.

locator.quote: in each of a constant fraction of the columns

entry.feedback: The phrasing can sound like a deterministic per-column necessity. The proof actually bounds a low-budget algorithm under a hard distribution by dividing columns into heavy ones and light ones whose correct address is unlikely to be guessed.
entry.why_it_matters: The informal statement is stronger than the event-based claim the lower-bound argument needs, and obscures why the direct product and the random planted column both matter.
entry.advice: Give this as a hard-distribution intuition, or say that a small total budget leaves most possible planted columns with too little address information. Avoid suggesting that every successful execution literally solves that many addresses.

locator.quote: reads its input one bit at a time

entry.feedback: The first sentence uses familiar classical reading language before giving the correct quantum oracle. A quantum query can have its index register in superposition; it does not reveal one classical bit to the algorithm at each step. This is conventional shorthand, but a more literal opening would remove the need to reinterpret it.
entry.why_it_matters: The paper immediately supplies the correct oracle, but the opening sentence makes the reader mentally undo a familiar misleading picture.
entry.advice: Introduce access through a bit oracle and the charge per oracle call. Reserve the language of reading a particular position for classical trees.

locator.section: §1 Introduction, Theorem 1 and the next paragraph
locator.quote: Taking $k=3$ in (2) gives exponent $10/3>3$

entry.feedback: The concrete k=3 consequence gives a quick reason this is a strict advance beyond the cubic relation, before the limiting quantifier argument.
entry.why_it_matters: It distinguishes refuting the cubic conjecture from the separate task of identifying the infimum of all universal exponents.
entry.advice: Keep the numerical witness here and the full fixed-k quantifier argument in §6.

locator.quote: This paper adds the following to the preprint.

entry.feedback: The four-part contribution paragraph mixes huge explicit constants, a common-circuit issue, counterexamples, two observations, the record, a uniform Forrelation bound and Lean. In the PDF it continues onto page 2 before the reader has seen the construction. These are not equally important reasons for a quantum specialist to read on.
entry.why_it_matters: The central algorithmic idea competes with a catalogue of supporting deliverables and refinements.
entry.advice: Lead with what the companion explains better: arbitrary-probability comparisons and the assembly of the two bounds. Move the numerical threshold and constant list next to the bounds they quantify; mention the other additions in a shorter contribution paragraph.

locator.quote: including a Forrelation lower bound uniform in $k$

entry.feedback: The uniform estimate is buried in the description of the record, although §5 later says it has a different proof route and a better k-dependence than the cited Bansal–Sinha estimate. That is a substantive quantitative refinement and should not first appear as a supporting-document feature.
entry.why_it_matters: A reader cannot separate the original separation theorem, the companion’s exposition, and the record’s additional quantitative work.
entry.advice: Name the uniform estimate as an additional result of the record, with its exact role in the growing-k remark. Preserve OpenAI’s credit for the original function and separation analysis; do not market the refinement as a new separation theorem.

locator.quote: Q=\widetilde O\bigl(m'+\sqrt{nm'}\bigr)

entry.feedback: The displayed cost suppresses Q(g) before the following sentence assumes it is polylogarithmic. With a general partial g, the evaluation contribution in the cited construction is m′Q(g), up to the stated logarithmic overhead.
entry.why_it_matters: A specialist checking the conversion has to supply a hypothesis retroactively; the display is otherwise not the count just described.
entry.advice: Move the polylogarithmic-Q(g) assumption before this display, or include Q(g) in the display and simplify afterwards. This is a local scope repair, not a challenge to the historical exponents.

locator.quote: Exponent $a$ with $R=Q^{a}$ (total $f$)

entry.feedback: The table heading uses equality for separation lower bounds, while its last row is an upper bound holding for every total function.
entry.why_it_matters: Two different logical directions are compressed into one heading, precisely where the reader is comparing the historical endpoints.
entry.advice: Label the separation rows by their achieved lower-bound exponent and put the universal upper bound in a visibly separate final row or sentence.

locator.quote: Tal's bound for $k$-fold Rorrelation

entry.feedback: Rorrelation appears before the text explains that it uses an orthogonal matrix rather than the explicit Walsh matrix. At this point it can look like a typographical variant of Forrelation.
entry.why_it_matters: A reader who knows Forrelation but has not followed the partial-separation literature may miss the distinction that later justifies the exact circuit.
entry.advice: Add a short parenthetical description on first use and let §1.3 carry the precise contrast.

locator.quote: the AND–OR recipe stops at the cube

entry.feedback: The current formulation correctly limits the barrier to the displayed construction and explains 5/2, 8/3 and 3 with one parameter c. This is a successful repair of the earlier historical discussion.
entry.why_it_matters: It explains what the new construction must change without asserting an impossibility theorem for all cheat-sheet ideas.
entry.advice: Keep the qualified scope and the common conversion calculation; do not replace it with an unsupported claim that all previous methods were incapable of going beyond three.

locator.quote: The answers $s_i=(P(A_{i,1}),\dots,P(A_{i,r}))$ select one cell

entry.feedback: The overview assigns an address to every column before mentioning that P is partial. On a total input some of these vectors do not exist.
entry.why_it_matters: This temporarily erases the off-promise case that is the source of the quantum algorithm’s difficulty.
entry.advice: Say at this first use that the true address exists when the column’s instances are promised. Later distinguish it from the decoder’s always-defined output label.

locator.quote: Column $i^\star$ is the winner:

entry.feedback: Figure 1 is an effective layout, but its internal label calls the r address blocks independent instances. The total function imposes no distribution or independence; only the hard distribution in §4 does. The word is not needed to explain disjoint coordinates.
entry.why_it_matters: The drawing can silently transfer a probabilistic assumption into the deterministic definition.
entry.advice: Use disjoint address blocks in the diagram and reserve independent for the sampled blocks of the lower-bound distribution. Keep the outward arrows and selected-cell emphasis.

locator.quote: which takes about $m^2$ queries.

entry.feedback: The heuristic makes the erased-zero obstacle resemble ordinary search over m² unrelated bits. Here there is one zero per dummy column and the planted index is independent; the key identity is E[Z]/m, not simply a generic OR lower bound.
entry.why_it_matters: The reader may misunderstand where the extra factor m comes from and why independence of the planted index is indispensable.
entry.advice: Give one clause connecting the heuristic to the number of columns whose zero has actually been discovered, with a forward reference to (11). Keep the detailed proof in §4.3.

locator.section: §1.2 Overview, order of the two mechanisms
locator.quote: For the classical lower bound we compare a zero-input

entry.feedback: The overview spends two dense paragraphs on the lower bound before explaining the nonstandard quantum search, even though the abstract and §3 identify that search as the point a quantum reader should inspect.
entry.why_it_matters: The motivating question—why cheap address decoding does not immediately make Grover search cheap—is answered late.
entry.advice: Consider introducing the nested-search cost and the comparison remedy immediately after Figure 1, then give the planted-distribution intuition. This is an ordering suggestion for this audience, not a demand that every version use the same order.

locator.quote: a total cost of about $\sqrt m\cdot\sqrt K\approx m$

entry.feedback: The failed nested-search count explains why the tournament is necessary. It turns a list of ingredients into an algorithmic design problem.
entry.why_it_matters: Without this bottleneck the reader might think the theorem follows by applying Grover search to the winner predicate.
entry.advice: Keep the cost comparison close to the first account of the algorithm and refer back to it when verification is deferred.

locator.section: §1.3 Relation to earlier constructions, comparison paragraph
locator.quote: king finding [@MPS2023] searches a fixed tournament

entry.feedback: The paragraph names king finding without specifying the output property. A king need only reach every vertex within two directed edges; a dominant candidate here must beat every opponent with high probability, and a listed candidate still needs verification.
entry.why_it_matters: The three tasks can look interchangeable simply because all use pairwise comparisons.
entry.advice: Give the output contract of king finding in a short clause, and compare contracts rather than only naming the graph models.

locator.section: §1.3 Relation to earlier constructions, comparison paragraph
locator.quote: Quantum search with bounded-error inputs [@HMW2003] likewise needs every comparison

entry.feedback: Høyer–Mosca–de Wolf formulate search over fixed target bits with bounded-error algorithms for those bits; their theorem is not specifically a comparison theorem. Here it can be used after a candidate is converted into a genuine verification predicate, but cannot simply interpret arbitrary loser-pair probabilities as noisy orientations.
entry.why_it_matters: The current shorthand risks making a precise hypothesis distinction sound like a blanket dismissal of bounded-error search.
entry.advice: Name the fixed target predicate and the cost of evaluating it. Explain that the obstacle is applying that primitive directly to the cheap pairwise comparison, rather than the impossibility of using bounded-error search anywhere.

locator.section: §1.3 Relation to earlier constructions, comparison paragraph
locator.quote: in each a comparison has a fixed intended outcome.

entry.feedback: This is the right contrast, but the paper leaves the relation among total orders, fixed tournaments, approximate fixed-edge evaluation and arbitrary pair probabilities entirely in a dense paragraph.
entry.why_it_matters: A reader must reconstruct which assumptions each cited algorithm shares with Proposition 3.
entry.advice: Use a small comparison of input contract, output contract and relevant invariant, or a short progression through those four cases. Keep it limited to the cited algorithms actually inspected.

locator.section: §1.3 Relation to earlier constructions, final paragraph
locator.quote: Every other link to the record points to a longer version

entry.feedback: The paragraph combining the roadmap, external inputs, record-only refinements, scope of every remaining link and the exposition reads like a navigation contract rather than the end of an introduction.
entry.why_it_matters: It delays §2 and asks the reader to retain a classification of links before encountering the corresponding mathematics.
entry.advice: Separate a short mathematical dependency statement from a one-sentence roadmap. Put detailed link classification in the record or repository navigation; keep no bureaucratic disclaimers in the paper.

locator.quote: It prepares $u$, applies the product in (3)

entry.feedback: The cost statement does not locally explain that each diagonal sign matrix uses one phase query to the standard bit oracle, while H, the uniform state and the projection are input-independent operations. That is the short bridge from the displayed linear algebra to O_k queries.
entry.why_it_matters: A specialist can supply the bridge, but a companion claiming to expose the argument should make the oracle accounting visible at its first essential use.
entry.advice: Add the one-query-per-sign-layer explanation and specify right-to-left application order. The original preprint supplies exactly these details in Lemma 2.1; no circuit diagram or gate count is needed.

locator.quote: The interference test of Aaronson and Ambainis

entry.feedback: The text explicitly says that the sign-sensitive interference test would also work and explains why promise membership is certified elsewhere. This prevents the projection experiment from being mistaken for a uniquely necessary decoder.
entry.why_it_matters: It connects the presentation to the form of Forrelation familiar to specialists and identifies which decoder property the construction consumes.
entry.advice: Keep this comparison and the on-promise/off-promise distinction, while avoiding an expanded survey of all equivalent tests.

locator.quote: An exact fan-in-two Boolean circuit $\mathcal C$

entry.feedback: The definition of S does not explicitly say whether it counts input nodes or only non-input gates, including the output gates. The cell size rS and K=r(S+2)+2m−1 later use the latter convention.
entry.why_it_matters: A reader checking the transcript length has to infer a counting convention that the original preprint states explicitly.
entry.advice: Define S as the number of non-input gates, including the output gates, once. This also explains why gate checks and the two output-value checks are distinct.

locator.quote: All of these are independent input bits.

entry.feedback: Independence is a property of a probability law, whereas this paragraph is defining the coordinates of a total Boolean function. The intended point is that cells contain separately supplied bits, rather than transcripts generated automatically from the A-blocks.
entry.why_it_matters: The phrasing is especially risky because independence later becomes a real hypothesis of the direct-product argument.
entry.advice: Say that these are separate, unconstrained input coordinates and that alleged transcripts may be wrong. Reserve probabilistic independence for §4.

locator.quote: both bounds in (2) are proved for the function built from it.

entry.feedback: Fixing the circuit before both analyses is a valuable precision point: changing the transcript circuit changes the total function’s coordinates.
entry.why_it_matters: It prevents a seemingly innocent combination of an upper bound for one construction with a lower bound for another.
entry.advice: Keep the mathematical point in §2. Later formal quantifiers can link back to it instead of restating the same reassurance several times.

locator.quote: so in terms of its input length

entry.feedback: The n-exponent is a useful secondary fact but is not used in either analysis or the optimal-power deduction. It appears between the function definition and the local-test mechanism, where the reader is trying to understand how a certificate can be checked cheaply.
entry.why_it_matters: It interrupts the construction-to-algorithm dependency with an asymptotic change of variable.
entry.advice: Move the input-length observation into a remark after the two complexity bounds or a short note at the end of §2. State explicitly that k is fixed in this conversion.

locator.quote: The circuit size enters the quantum bound only through the cost $\sqrt K$

entry.feedback: This sentence is an excellent explanation of why the circuit must be small even though the quantum algorithm does not evaluate all its gates directly.
entry.why_it_matters: It separates the cost of generating a certificate from the cost of checking a supplied transcript.
entry.advice: Keep this sentence at the end of the local-test paragraph; it is more useful than additional exact gate-count arithmetic.

locator.quote: Each trial chooses, with probability $1/2$ each

entry.feedback: Round six planned a two-sentence amplification sketch. The current proof still walks through M, a two-case success estimate, 9/20, 9/40 and repeated trials before the new comparison mechanism appears. Those constants are standard supporting machinery, while the exact successful-label law is the property later used.
entry.why_it_matters: A quantum specialist spends attention on a familiar implementation before reaching the novel invariant; the priority of the previous revision has not fully survived.
entry.advice: Retain the fixed-cap contract, state preservation and a concise explanation of randomized Grover counts plus fresh retries. Leave the numerical trial calculation in record §5.1 and cite BHMT/BBHT locally.

locator.quote: Search with an unknown success probability bounds its cost only in expectation

entry.feedback: The sentence is broader than its cited result. BHMT Theorem 3 is an expected-cost QSearch algorithm; fixed timeouts and bounded-error worst-case search are already standard in BBHT and Dürr–Høyer. A known lower threshold on p allows the capped form used here.
entry.why_it_matters: The wording can make a routine truncation device sound like a previously unavailable feature of quantum search.
entry.advice: Refer specifically to the untruncated QSearch theorem being contrasted, and say what the threshold γ and fixed retry budget add for this application. Do not claim that unknown-p search in general only has expected bounds.

locator.quote: Below we use only the distribution of the label measured after a success

entry.feedback: This sentence makes the operational need clear without denying the stronger state-preserving mathematical lemma. It is a successful correction of the earlier conflation.
entry.why_it_matters: The reader can follow the sampler using ordinary conditional probabilities once the coherent trial is finished.
entry.advice: Keep it adjacent to the lemma, and make the record’s corresponding finite-label discussion agree with the separate measured/reset implementation described in §7.

locator.quote: For an unordered pair $\{i,j\}$, we sort the indices

entry.feedback: Sorting the pair before running one circuit is the right concrete reason for a_ij+a_ji=1. Complementarity is a semantic property of the same experiment, not an assumption about two independently designed decoders.
entry.why_it_matters: The drift identity depends exactly on this symmetry, even for off-promise rivals.
entry.advice: Preserve the construction and the explicit self-loss convention through compression.

locator.quote: If exactly one column disqualifies the other, it is the victor;

entry.feedback: This rule has two binary observations and two tie cases, but it is encoded in a long procedural sentence. A reader checking the tie-break counterexample must reconstruct the four possible outputs.
entry.why_it_matters: It is easy to reverse which pointer bit disqualifies which column.
entry.advice: Give a compact four-case description, or state the two pointer bits first and then the winning condition. Link the smallest-index tie to the false-dominant example in Appendix A.

locator.quote: The decoded labels stay in orthogonal registers

entry.feedback: This explicitly justifies transferring the measured decoder probabilities into the coherent comparison circuit. It is mathematical content, not formalisation bookkeeping.
entry.why_it_matters: Without retained labels, erasing or merging branches could alter the comparison amplitudes and invalidate the later product law.
entry.advice: Keep the sentence and the retained-workspace requirement in Proposition 3.

locator.quote: One comparison costs $c=O_k(\ell\log\ell)$ queries.

entry.feedback: The cost is correct from the displayed r and ε, but the paper never explicitly connects the relatively weak ε=Θ(1/log m) guarantee to the fact that comparisons are sampled as their actual probability laws. Readers accustomed to approximate-oracle composition may expect error reduction proportional to the total number of coherent calls.
entry.why_it_matters: This is one of the most instructive differences from treating the circuit as an approximate fixed predicate.
entry.advice: Explain that no claim is made that every comparison call is correct: a_ij are exact circuit probabilities, and only the winner’s product weight needs the 1−ε bound over T pivots. This resolves a likely error-budget question without adding another union bound.

locator.quote: A quantum algorithm with $O(c\sqrt m\,T^2\log T)$ queries

entry.feedback: The proposition gives the crucial contract but the actual algorithm is dispersed among the ideal-process, exact-sampling and coupling paragraphs. A reader has to reconstruct when the pivot list is updated, when measurement occurs and what is returned on failure.
entry.why_it_matters: This adds avoidable reconstruction work to the one algorithm the specialist came to understand.
entry.advice: Put a brief numbered description beside the proposition: initial empty list; construct the trial from the measured history; amplify and measure; append or stop; return the list after at most T stages. Keep the proofs in the existing paragraphs.

locator.quote: We replace membership in that set by the weight

entry.feedback: The set-to-weight relationship is now stated explicitly and is the best connection to the 2026 candidate-comparison literature.
entry.why_it_matters: It shows how the familiar surviving-set invariant changes when loser comparisons do not encode fixed edges.
entry.advice: Preserve this explanation and add a genuinely fractional example if space permits; do not re-raise the already fixed complaint that the relationship is absent.

locator.quote: the probability that $i$ beats every pivot

entry.feedback: This phrase should be read as the probability for fresh comparison trials conditional on a fixed input and already measured pivot history. It is not a statement that the events in the adaptive ideal process are unconditionally independent.
entry.why_it_matters: The product notation invites precisely the independence confusion that the fresh-workspace construction later resolves.
entry.advice: Add the conditional/fresh-trial qualification here, then let the tensor-product calculation establish it. No independence assumption on the input is involved.

locator.quote: After $T$ steps $\mathbb EW\le m2^{-T}$.

entry.feedback: The process is defined to stop when W=0, but this sentence refers to a value after T steps. The intended convention is that zero weight remains zero after stopping.
entry.why_it_matters: The probabilistic argument is sound, but a proof-oriented reader momentarily has to complete the stopped process.
entry.advice: Declare the stopped state absorbing, or write the bound for W after padding stopped runs by zeros. A short clause is enough.

locator.quote: No order or transitivity enters, so cycles among losers do no harm.

entry.feedback: The statement comes immediately after the pairing identity that proves it. This is persuasive mathematical exposition: the allowed pathology is explained by the proof, not merely asserted.
entry.why_it_matters: It identifies the invariant responsible for generality and helps a reader see why a three-cycle is harmless.
entry.advice: Keep the identity and this consequence next to one another.

locator.quote: The algorithm never computes the weights.

entry.feedback: This crucial statement is easy to skim past. A reader may otherwise imagine amplitude estimation of every a_ij followed by a classical weighted sample, which would destroy the query bound.
entry.why_it_matters: It is the implementation insight that converts the classical ideal process into a cheap quantum routine.
entry.advice: Give the sentence more prominence and tie it directly to the success-and-label mass w_i/m. A small state/flag schematic would help more than a second static picture of the input.

locator.quote: \frac1{\sqrt m}\sum_{i=1}^m|i\rangle\bigotimes_{b=1}^{n}|\phi(i,\rho_b)\rangle

entry.feedback: The expert paper gives the exact state and mass computation but no finite example with fractional a_ij. The exposition’s new sampled stage uses only deterministic comparisons, so following the cross-document route still does not exhibit the feature that distinguishes the theorem from fixed-tournament search.
entry.why_it_matters: The algebra is correct, but the reader never sees the weighted generalisation do something a surviving set cannot.
entry.advice: Add or point to a tiny admissible comparison-probability matrix with a dominant candidate and a fractional loser pair, and trace one measured pivot, the resulting nonbinary weights, the total success probability and the conditional label law. Label it as an example of Proposition 3 unless a board realisation is actually supplied. One concrete abstract instance has dominant vertex 1, a_1j=1 for j≠1, a_23=1/3, a_24=3/4, a_34=2/5, reverse probabilities complementary, and diagonal zero. After pivot 2, weights are (1,0,2/3,1/4), success probability is 23/48, and the conditional label law is (12/23,0,8/23,3/23). These numbers illustrate the existing abstract proposition; they are not asserted to be realised by the supplied four-column board.

locator.quote: on reported failure we stop and return the list.

entry.feedback: Stopping with the current list is essential for zero inputs and for histories after a dominant candidate has already been selected.
entry.why_it_matters: It avoids silently assuming a solution exists for every amplification call or letting an unknown-probability search run indefinitely.
entry.advice: Keep the stopped-list behaviour visible in any algorithm summary.

locator.quote: The failure probabilities may depend on the history

entry.feedback: This is the right reason to couple conditional on the full past rather than condition globally on all stages succeeding. Exact labels at each successful stage do not make an all-success conditioned history unbiased.
entry.why_it_matters: It protects the most delicate probabilistic transfer in the upper bound.
entry.advice: Preserve the stagewise coupling and the fact that a failure after inclusion cannot remove the winner; avoid compressing it to a bare union-bound slogan.

locator.quote: Stage $n$ costs $O(c(n+1)\sqrt m\log(1/\varepsilon))$

entry.feedback: The current indexing uses n for the number of previous pivots, while earlier n denoted total input length. The +1 is also padding relative to n comparison workspaces and is not explained.
entry.why_it_matters: Neither issue changes the bound, but the reader must resolve a needless symbol collision while checking the only nontrivial query sum.
entry.advice: Use a stage/history index such as s consistently in this subsection and say the +1 is harmless padding, including the empty history. Preparing the uniform initial state is input-independent and costs no input queries.

locator.quote: A column that beats every rival with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$ need not win

entry.feedback: The warning is correct, but its justification is relegated to row 3 of a table after the references. This is the precise reason the algorithm returns a list for verification rather than deciding acceptance from its tournament.
entry.why_it_matters: A quantum reader may see verification as routine overhead rather than the operation that makes the algorithm valid on every input.
entry.advice: Give the one-sentence all-one, smallest-index false-certificate example here, with the detailed counterexample retained in Appendix A. Link it to the different meanings of comparison dominance and satisfying the total function.

locator.quote: We reject the candidate if a failing test is found and accept it otherwise

entry.feedback: The verifier treats reported failure of the search as acceptance of the candidate. That is correct, but the words failure and success now reverse their meaning relative to candidate validity.
entry.why_it_matters: A reader can momentarily confuse the search’s failure flag with an unreliable candidate or with a failure to run the algorithm.
entry.advice: Name the search output as a detected violation versus no violation detected, and immediately attach the two guarantees: a true certificate has no violation; a false certificate escapes detection with probability at most ε.

locator.quote: the winner is accepted whenever its address is decoded correctly.

entry.feedback: The ensuing one-input bound uses only one fresh decoding error, not T verification errors. This is a useful asymmetry, but the explanation is implicit.
entry.why_it_matters: A reader may think the union bound is missing a term or try to add errors for accepting nonwinners on an input whose correct answer is already one.
entry.advice: Say that false positives on a one-input cannot hurt the decision and that, conditional on reaching the listed winner, its fresh decoder has failure probability at most ε for every prior history.

locator.quote: The exponent six in (2) comes from a deliberately loose count

entry.feedback: The paragraph derives the loose exponent through inflated log bounds after giving the sharper comparison cost and the tournament proposition. It forces the reader to switch accounting conventions solely to match a stated constant package.
entry.why_it_matters: The main algorithmic cost is harder to remember than it needs to be, and routine padding receives more space than the operational sampler.
entry.advice: Keep a small ledger of comparison, tournament and verification costs, then state that the explicit bound is padded to log^6 for the record’s constants. Move the trial-by-trial padding calculation to record §5.4 as intended in round six.

locator.quote: by compactness the best worst-case success is attained

entry.feedback: The compactness and minimax justification is inserted into an otherwise algorithmic transition as a long final sentence. It is mathematically legitimate, but its placement makes the reader work through the existence of μ before seeing what μ will be used to hide.
entry.why_it_matters: This slows a quantum specialist entering the classical half without helping them retain the construction.
entry.advice: Introduce μ and its depth-L hardness property first, then give the finite minimax justification in a short parenthesis or immediately following sentence. Keep the strict L<R(P) hypothesis.

locator.quote: We work with unnormalised measures, so that branches of probability zero need no conditioning.

entry.feedback: This is an economical explanation of the proof’s choice of formalism. The leaf factorisation and one-factor update are then enough to see why adaptive interleaving does not break the product.
entry.why_it_matters: A quantum reader gets a complete lower-bound ingredient without a detour into a general direct-product theorem.
entry.advice: Keep this proof and the joint-independence hypothesis; its compactness is a good model for trimming the standard amplification calculation.

locator.quote: Drucker's Theorem 1.1

entry.feedback: The nearby discussion of exact β^r versus 2β^r is a useful historical clarification, but the full parameter substitution competes with the conclusion of the lemma.
entry.why_it_matters: The specialist needs to know that the general theorem would suffice; they do not need to stop the proof to audit a second proof route.
entry.advice: Keep the one-sentence sufficiency observation and send the explicit substitution to the record. Do not revive the previous incorrect suggestion that a global-budget theorem cannot apply.

locator.quote: leaves every cell blank, with all its bits zero.

entry.feedback: Blank is helpfully defined as a fixed bit string, but a later query to the selected cell is treated as a possible discrepancy even when that particular bit agrees with zero in the planted input.
entry.why_it_matters: A careful reader may try to interpret cell access as an exact detection event and wonder where an occupancy flag is stored.
entry.advice: Say once that touching the cell is a sufficient event to cover all possible discrepancies, not that every such query detects the plant. No extra marker bit is present or needed.

locator.quote: They differ only at the erased zero

entry.feedback: Figure 2 and its caption identify the two places in which the coupled inputs can differ and state that the address blocks are shared. This gives the lower-bound proof a concrete causal structure.
entry.why_it_matters: It makes the two subsequent probability estimates an exhaustive list of possible discrepancy events. The events can overlap, so their probabilities are combined by a union bound.
entry.advice: Keep the shared-data statement and the precise cell-block versus single-bit distinction.

locator.quote: since $J_i$ is uniform on the unqueried rows

entry.feedback: The uniformity claim is valid before the first discovery of that column’s zero and for a newly queried row. As written, the preceding sentence speaks of a query with fewer than m/2 rows queried, which could include a repeated query to a zero already discovered.
entry.why_it_matters: The proof counts discoveries, so the argument is repairable without changing the estimate, but the conditional-probability sentence is wider than its intended event.
entry.advice: Make first discovery explicit and either remove repeat queries or state that they contribute no new discoveries. This is a local event-description repair.

locator.quote: A sharper count, which we cite from

entry.feedback: The sharper constant is immediately declared unnecessary. Its appearance in the short proof invites a detour from the two-event argument to a refinement that changes neither exponent nor contradiction.
entry.why_it_matters: It breaks the proof’s pace without strengthening the claim this paper is using.
entry.advice: Keep the refinement in the record and, if desired, place its link in a final remark after the lower bound rather than inside the erased-zero estimate.

locator.quote: The position of a query already names an address:

entry.feedback: This is the clearest sentence in the classical mechanism. It explains why even a query to a blank cell can be converted into a predictor, before any cell contents are read.
entry.why_it_matters: It makes the simulation and direct-product application comprehensible to a reader coming from the quantum half.
entry.advice: Keep the sentence before the simulator, and retain the explicit jointly independent free information.

locator.quote: Fix a column $i$ and a time $\tau

entry.feedback: The simulator paragraph contains free information, emulation, a total-query cutoff, output convention, per-instance cap implication and event inclusion in one long block. The proof is correct in structure, but the inclusion that yields (12) is difficult to isolate.

entry.feedback: This is an effective contract boundary. locator.quote: Put $c=\delta^2=2^{-10k}$.

entry.feedback: This is where the cost hidden by O_k becomes concrete, but its role is not stated. That distinction is central to why fixed-k exponent exclusion is easy and a growing-k schedule needs the separate accounting in §7.3.
entry.why_it_matters: “Cheap quantum decoder” can be heard as uniformly cheap in every parameter; the record itself later pays for the factor 2^(10k).

locator.quote: Every address, flag and count register is retained.

entry.feedback: The construction is correct, but the purpose of retaining this much information is still implicit. This is a bounded-error output-bit preparation, not a clean exact oracle for P. Its complete inverse is available because the trial histories remain. That is the interface used inside a comparison and, in turn, inside amplitude amplification.
entry.why_it_matters: A reader may attempt to measure each trial or copy a noisy answer and discard the rest, then unknowingly change the subroutine available to the tournament.
entry.advice: Connect this sentence directly to the later comparison circuit and its inverse. Contrast the exact compute–copy–uncompute argument for local tests in §4.6 with this noisy decoder only to explain the necessary retained workspace.

the ideal process selects
$s$ within three pivots with probability one.

entry.feedback: The text is correct, but the cost consequence is easy to miss: each new stage preparation rebuilds comparisons against the entire stored pivot history. It does not continue from a previous collapsed comparison register. The same rebuild is repeated inside the bounded amplifier.
entry.why_it_matters: This is the operational reason for the sum of history lengths and hence T squared. Without it, the final query bound looks like a padding artifact.

locator.quote: It follows from the phase-independent successful-state assertion by measuring the label.

entry.feedback: As ordinary mathematics this implication is right. In the preceding paragraph, however, the subject has become “The compiled version”, and the sentence can be read as saying that its source theorem is derived from the retained-state physical implementation. The current companion §7 explicitly says the formal upper bound uses a separate procedure that measures the label and resets its workspace. Appendix G.7 also distinguishes the routes. Those statements should not be left for the reader to reconcile.

entry.advice: Separate the ordinary derivation of the measured law from the description of the independent measure/reset implementation. State that both provide the law needed here, without identifying their returned states or implying a source dependency that the record itself says is absent.

locator.quote: The independence belongs to the construction of the coupling

entry.feedback: This is the right explanation of the auxiliary independent Bernoulli variable. The implementation need not have an input-independent failure rate or generate an ideal pivot independently of its physical failure event; the exact factorized output law permits this probability-space representation.
entry.why_it_matters: It prevents an otherwise plausible objection that adaptive stage failures invalidate the coupling.
entry.advice: Keep this sentence and the conditioning on the complete common history. This is one of the record’s clearest improvements over a compressed union-bound explanation.

locator.quote: The argument stops charging failures once $s$ has appeared.

entry.feedback: This stopping point is essential. After the dominant vertex is sampled its own weight becomes zero, so no lower bound on the next stage’s success probability need remain. Retaining s in the classical list is enough for the task.
entry.why_it_matters: A global bound on failure at every later stage would be false in general; the record correctly proves only the histories the inclusion argument needs.
entry.advice: Keep it immediately after the miss bound, and show it in the numerical example as suggested separately.

locator.quote: On reported failure we stop and return the current list

entry.feedback: “Failure” denotes at least three different events in this section: a failed local test, amplification returning no successful sample, and failure of the final decision algorithm. In verification, a failure of the amplifier means accepting the candidate; in the tournament it means returning the list. The prose is individually correct, but the same word changes logical polarity at the section boundary.
entry.why_it_matters: The reader can reverse the one-sided verifier guarantee or add the wrong error event when reconstructing the total-error proof.
entry.advice: Give a compact table of the success flag, returned failure symbol and caller action for tournament sampling and failed-test search. Keep epsilon budgets alongside those actions rather than adding another general disclaimer.

Likewise ell is a Grover iteration count in §5.1 and the pointer width elsewhere. Each local definition is recoverable, but a reader crossing subsection boundaries has to reset two central symbols.

entry.advice: Use distinct local symbols for history length and iteration number, while retaining t and ell for the construction parameters. This is a notation edit, not a change to any formula.

locator.quote: If exactly one column is disqualified, the other wins

entry.feedback: The two pointer directions and the wording “disqualifies” versus “is disqualified” require a careful reread. The text correctly sorts the unordered pair and resolves both ties, but the four Boolean cases are easier to inspect than two long sentences describing them.
entry.why_it_matters: A reversed pointer direction would destroy the winner-only robustness argument, so this is worth making visually checkable.
entry.advice: Consider a four-row table keyed by the two observed target bits, with the selected column and the tie convention. Refer to that table in the proof of complementarity; keep the sorted-pair convention explicit.

locator.quote: The result is a classical mixture over the decoded labels

entry.feedback: The surrounding argument is about measurement probabilities, but this sentence calls the result itself a classical mixture. The retained-label circuit is still a pure coherent preparation before measurement. Orthogonality makes the probability of the selected comparison outcome equal a sum over label blocks; it does not turn the global state into a classical mixture.
entry.why_it_matters: This wording undermines the careful distinction between retained coherent workspaces and measured/reset output elsewhere in the same section.
entry.advice: Name the comparison output law, or the probability calculation, as the classical mixture. Keep the state description coherent and retain the block-diagonal projection explanation. This is a wording correction, not a counterexample to the probability calculation.

locator.quote: c=O_k(r\ln(r/\varepsilon)+\ell)= (\log m)^{O_k(1)}

entry.feedback: The cost immediately retreats to an unspecified polylogarithm even though the already defined parameters give the more transparent O_k(ell log ell) expression used in the current companion. That transparent expression helps a reader distinguish the algorithm’s natural count from the deliberately enlarged polynomial count used to obtain exponent six.
entry.why_it_matters: The longer record is less informative than its short derivative about where the logarithmic losses actually enter.
entry.advice: Carry the existing O_k(ell log ell) simplification into this cost summary and then explicitly say when the later accounting enlarges it. Do not optimize the algorithm or claim a new bound.

locator.quote: any earlier acceptance already gives the correct output one.

entry.feedback: This sentence cleanly explains why a false acceptance of an earlier nonwinner does not count as a decision error on a one-input. The algorithm is deciding F, not promising to output a valid winning certificate. The argument therefore needs only the probability that the true winner is missing or is rejected when reached.
entry.why_it_matters: It avoids paying for irrelevant bad events and keeps the claimed output task precise.
entry.advice: Keep it. If the implementation is later presented as a witness-finding algorithm, that would require a different stated guarantee; the present exposition should continue to describe the Boolean decision task.

locator.quote: A nonwinner has at least one failed test at every address

entry.feedback: The universal quantifier over addresses is what makes conditioning on an arbitrary decoder output harmless. It follows from semantic local-test equivalence, not from any accuracy assertion about the nonwinner’s Forrelation inputs. This is the right place to close the all-input correctness argument.
entry.why_it_matters: A weaker statement only about a true address would not cover columns containing unpromised inputs.
entry.advice: Preserve the quantifier and its short proof before averaging over the measured address. It is more important than the precise constant in the search cap.

locator.quote: An abstract read consists of a coordinate function on basis labels

entry.feedback: The ordinary two-query controlled-read construction immediately above already explains how the algorithm uses the input oracle. This paragraph then specifies the source’s signed involution interface, embeddings and continuation machinery in the middle of query accounting. Those details matter to a compiler audit, but the algorithmic argument has no unexplained oracle operation left at this point.
entry.why_it_matters: The main proof again changes from mathematics into an API description just before the reader expects the total count.
entry.advice: Keep the load–use–unload calculation and its two-query conclusion in §5.4. Move the abstract-read representation to the formal-model destination, with a backlink from the finite budget. Preserve the distinction between a measure/reset continuation and a retained quantum output.

locator.quote: Using $\ln(1/\varepsilon)\leq1/\varepsilon$

entry.feedback: This deliberate enlargement is the reason the displayed exponent six should not be read as an inherent feature of the construction. The companion says so directly. The record instead presents several pages of scalar bounds before calling the final constant deliberately loose, which can leave the role of the exponent itself unclear.
entry.why_it_matters: An expert may spend time trying to explain a log loss that was introduced only to simplify uniform finite accounting.
entry.advice: Say before the substitution that the following calculation chooses a convenient fixed logarithmic power and is not an optimization claim. Keep the explicit finite budget as the object being bounded and show which factors are deliberately enlarged.

locator.quote: it gives no bound on the number of elementary gates or the amount of workspace

entry.feedback: This is a useful substantive limitation of the theorem. The enormous addressed input and retained fresh registers do not violate query complexity, because input-independent computation and workspace are free in the model.
entry.why_it_matters: Readers coming from quantum algorithms with gate or memory estimates otherwise have an obvious unanswered resource question.
entry.advice: Keep this concise explanation in the main text. It does more work than a generic warning about practicality and needs no speculative discussion of hardware.

locator.quote: The Lean proof of Theorem 1.1 takes a slightly different route

entry.feedback: The explanation says that the different route runs the tournament and verifies the listed candidates in sequence, but §5.3 already describes exactly that overall algorithm. What changes is the form of the formal theorem: an acceptance-bit continuation is proved directly, instead of first exposing a list-membership witness.
entry.why_it_matters: The reader may infer that there are two mathematically different evaluation algorithms and wonder which one has the stated cost and error.
entry.advice: Describe the distinction as a proof/output-interface distinction. Then explain why the continuation induction recovers the same Boolean decision guarantee. Keep the full induction for readers following the formal headline.

entry.feedback: The tournament appends new pivots to a chronological list, while this recurrence prepends i using the source-list notation. The weight product and eventual “some verifier accepts” event are insensitive to that storage order, but the text does not say whether L is now stored in reverse chronological order.
entry.why_it_matters: A reader translating the recurrence into the earlier algorithm can think that the history order or verification order has silently changed.
entry.advice: State the storage convention at the first cons operation, or keep append notation throughout the ordinary proof. Explain the harmless order invariance rather than leaving it to reconstruction.

locator.quote: gives a lower bound $Q=

entry.feedback: Q has denoted quantum query complexity throughout the record, but here it is reused for a scalar lower estimate in a recurrence about success probability. The local equality defines it, so this is not a mathematical error; it is an avoidable interruption in a technically dense passage.
entry.why_it_matters: The reader must briefly unlearn the paper’s most important notation at the point where a signed lower bound is being manipulated.
entry.advice: Rename this local quantity to a neutral bound symbol and retain the separate nonnegative/negative cases in the argument.

locator.section: §5.5, handling a potentially negative lower estimate
locator.quote: We always have $Q\leq1-\varepsilon$, even when $Q$ is negative.

entry.feedback: The signed-estimate check is worth preserving. Multiplying an inductive lower bound by a success probability and then subtracting a failure penalty is a place where a handwave can reverse the needed inequality. The proof explicitly handles the negative case instead of assuming the lower estimate is a probability.
entry.why_it_matters: This small paragraph supplies the exact justification a referee needs for the continuation induction.
entry.advice: Keep the argument, with the local scalar renamed as suggested separately. It is an example of useful detail rather than routine constant arithmetic.

locator.quote: We now choose $k=\lfloor\sqrt{t/20}\rfloor$

entry.feedback: The choice is motivated only after a long expansion of C_k and another floor calculation. The illuminating tradeoff appears later as 40k+ell/k: increasing k reduces the classical exponent deficit but increases the quantum decoder overhead. That balance explains the square-root schedule.
entry.why_it_matters: The reader initially receives a parameter choice as a numerical trick rather than a consequence of the two costs competing.
entry.advice: Preview the competing terms before expanding the constant, then retain the exact derivation that validates the existing schedule. This would explain the present result without proposing a different schedule or stronger theorem.

locator.quote: The chain gives the constant $474$; we state $508$, the value used in the specialist companion.

entry.feedback: This sentence explains an editorial reconciliation rather than a mathematical necessity. The proof legitimately relaxes one constant to another, but saying it does so because another document already uses that number makes the derivation sound driven by synchronization with a draft.
entry.why_it_matters: It draws attention away from the actual conservative inequality and makes the reader wonder whether the constants were chosen independently of the proof.
entry.advice: Describe 508 simply as a convenient common upper bound, with any cross-document reconciliation retained in revision notes. Keep all three documents on the same stated bound.

locator.quote: The prefactor can be checked on two bits.

entry.feedback: The sensitivity matrix, its masks and the progress drop are useful new parts of this check. The complete one-query parity-state derivation is already given in §2.6, however, and is repeated here before the genuinely relevant matrix calculation.
entry.why_it_matters: The appendix makes a careful diagnostic feel longer than its new mathematical content requires.
entry.advice: Refer back to the exact parity algorithm in §2.6 and keep the explicit adversary matrix, eigenvalues and progress drop here. The source-prefactor comparison remains recoverable without repeating the entire preparation.

locator.quote: A separate older annex transcription inserted an extra square root around the entire denominator.

entry.feedback: The distinction between an error in an earlier annex transcription and the printed source discrepancy is useful provenance, but it interrupts the mathematical witness. A first-time reader has not seen that older annex and does not need its correction history to understand the factor-two issue.
entry.why_it_matters: A clear exact example turns into a report about the project’s earlier debugging session.
entry.advice: Keep the edition-specific claim, exact counterexample and limit of the conclusion in Appendix A. Move the older-transcription chronology to execution/source-comparison notes rather than expanding it in the proof.

locator.quote: Pre-success state: m^{-1/2} sum_{i=1}^m |i> tensor_{b=1}^t |phi(i,p_b)>.

entry.feedback: The catalogue’s mathematical content is useful, but its ASCII-style expressions and raw claim-name headings are much harder to read than the surrounding typeset record. A reader who follows a mathematical claim into the catalogue encounters a serialization format rather than a concise mathematical statement.
entry.why_it_matters: The catalogue is intended to reduce recovery cost, but the notation translation becomes an extra step before following its proof links.
entry.advice: Give entries readable mathematical titles and rendered notation while retaining their exact IDs as anchors. Preserve the machine-readable catalogue separately if it is needed by tooling.

locator.quote: [§5.2](#upper-continuation-induction)

entry.feedback: The anchor resolves to the continuation induction, but that passage is now in §5.5. The same stale visible label appears in the catalogue’s claim-error entry. The link technically works, which is why checking only anchor existence misses the defect.
entry.why_it_matters: A reader switching between printed sections and hyperlinks is told two different locations for the same argument.
entry.advice: Update the displayed section labels from the current heading tree and check the other catalogue links semantically. This is separate from the stale companion-section references near the record’s beginning.

locator.quote: This account is written for a graduate student who knows the query models above

entry.feedback: The paragraph now honestly declares substantial prerequisites, but it answers the previous review by narrowing the audience. The packet asks for a mathematician from another field or a strong undergraduate who has not studied query complexity. Knowing the oracle models, unknown-probability amplification, uncomputation, Yao and adaptive decision-tree conditioning is already a substantial quantum-query course. This is a scope mismatch, not a request to delete the useful prerequisite disclosure.
entry.why_it_matters: The intended newcomer can be excluded before the first example, even though the main construction can be taught with several of these results stated as precise tools.
entry.advice: Keep the reader promised by the assignment. Teach the few operations actually used, and state the deeper results as inputs with their contracts. Keep the more demanding route available as a quantum-course reading route. The existing exposition skill explicitly forbids treating stronger prerequisites as completion of a fixed-audience task.

locator.quote: A quantum algorithm reads through the oracle $O_x|j,b,w\rangle=|j,b\oplus x_j,w\rangle$

entry.feedback: The model arrives as a ket transformation in the third sentence, before the reader is told what a register or an oracle call is. Saying that it acts on a superposition can easily suggest that one query returns a readable list of all input bits. The text also leaves the distinction between a query and an ordinary computational gate implicit.
entry.why_it_matters: Every later cheap quantum step depends on counting oracle invocations, not on getting all the bit values for free.
entry.advice: At first use, identify j as an address, b as a one-bit answer register, and w as temporary memory; say that one invocation counts as one query and that measuring the resulting state does not reveal all x_j. State that input-independent computation is not charged. A short four-position state example would do more than additional general quantum prose.

locator.quote: some constant }C\text{ gives }R(f)\le C\,(1+Q(f))^{\alpha}

entry.feedback: The displayed infimum is correct, but its most consequential quantifier is left to the notation: C must work for every total function and every input length. A reader may confuse that universal C with the k-dependent C_k in the very next display, or think the theorem compares two algorithms for one fixed input length.
entry.why_it_matters: Without the universal scope, choosing a constant after seeing a function makes the optimal-exponent question trivial.
entry.advice: Give the quantifier one ordinary sentence before the display: the same multiplicative constant must work throughout the class. Then explicitly separate it from constants attached to a fixed construction parameter. Explain the harmless 1+Q convention only if needed to avoid a question about Q=0.

locator.quote: R\approx m^{2-1/k}=(\sqrt m)^{4-2/k}\approx Q^{4-2/k}

entry.feedback: The approximation chain is visually stronger than the established claims. The argument supplies an upper bound on Q and a lower bound on R; it does not establish that either displayed algorithm is optimal for this particular family. The use of approximately equal signs suppresses both logarithms and the direction of the inequalities.
entry.why_it_matters: A newcomer may leave believing an exact relationship or matching family bounds have been proved, rather than a separation sufficient to exclude smaller universal powers.
entry.advice: Preserve the one-line arithmetic, but label it explicitly as comparing the proved lower and upper scales. Use directional language or inequalities when moving from those scales to R versus Q. The final ratio argument already has the correct logic.

locator.section: Introduction: theorem before a numerical foothold
locator.quote: A single $k$ reaches only the exponent $4-2/k$

entry.feedback: The first two pages contain k, m, L, r and an infimum but no concrete exponent value. The later k=3 example comes only in Section 6. A new reader is asked to feel why this is an advance over quadratic and cubic separation before seeing one instance of the arithmetic.
entry.why_it_matters: The title promises an explanation of four, while the opening can look like a collection of unrelated parameters.
entry.advice: At this first occurrence, use one existing specialization, such as fixed k=3 giving exponent 10/3 up to the displayed losses, and then point out what increases as k increases. This is substitution into the stated bounds, not an additional result.

locator.quote: a certificate that $F=1$ sits in one of them

entry.feedback: Certificate is doing substantial work before it has a definition. In query complexity it is a set of revealed input bits forcing an answer, while the later cell stores proposed circuit values and pointers that still require checking. A student may read the cell itself as an externally trusted proof.
entry.why_it_matters: The construction relies on distinguishing stored claims from a verified winning certificate, especially on malformed inputs.
entry.advice: Define a certificate in one elementary example or a parenthetical sentence, then call a cell a proposed certificate until its local tests pass. Keep the distinction between input data and proof of its correctness consistent through the column construction.

locator.quote: Tal reached $8/3-o(1)$

entry.feedback: The history lists 5/2, 8/3 and 3, but only the final cubic ceiling receives a mechanism. Tal appears as a number in a chronology. A quantum reader wants to know whether each gain came from a better partial-function separation, a different totalization, or a different evaluation algorithm.
entry.why_it_matters: The sequence can be memorized without understanding which bottleneck the present tournament removes.
entry.advice: Either compress the intermediate numerical history and link to the companion, or attach one concrete role to each retained milestone. Keep the detailed old-route-versus-new-route arithmetic, which is the part that teaches something.

locator.quote: The cheat-sheet function composes a partial function $g$ on $n$ bits with AND-OR

entry.feedback: Composition has a direction, and n is used both for the logical input size of g and for the side length of a gadget. A newcomer cannot tell from this sentence whether g replaces each AND-OR bit or AND-OR replaces each input bit of g. The subsequent product n^2 R(g) assumes the latter construction.
entry.why_it_matters: The cubic-ceiling calculation is one of the best ideas in the exposition, but its scaling is difficult to reconstruct from the prose alone.
entry.advice: Say which logical bits are replaced by which gadgets, and identify the gadget input count separately from the logical input count. A small block-of-blocks sketch or the notation g composed with AND-OR would settle the direction before the cost multiplication.

locator.quote: Section 1 computes $k$-fold Forrelation on three eight-bit inputs

entry.feedback: The first concrete matrix begins on PDF page 3, after nearly two pages of model definitions, an infimum, exact constants, construction overview, milestone history, an AND-OR comparison, prerequisites and a full route map. The examples-first title is therefore asking the reader to wait through a specialist-style introduction before its main teaching device begins.
entry.why_it_matters: The opening demands more working memory than the small example would require and risks losing exactly the intended non-specialist reader.
entry.advice: Keep the question, the directional exponent arithmetic and a short route map at the entrance. Move the long historical comparison to the point where the failed direct search is explained, or offer it as a marked side route. This is an ordering recommendation, not a request to remove the theorem from page one.

locator.quote: apply the signs $z_2$ with one query

entry.feedback: This is the first consequential use of phase kickback, but the opening oracle writes x_j into an answer bit. The missing bridge is exactly how that bit-query oracle multiplies an address amplitude by (-1)^{x_j} while retaining the address. Calling it phase kickback in Section 3 arrives after the reader has already needed it.
entry.why_it_matters: The two-query claim can look like a new, more powerful oracle than the one defined at the beginning.
entry.advice: Give the one-line action on an answer qubit prepared in the minus state, and explain that the answer register factors back out. Also say that the Walsh transform and projection are input-independent operations, hence cost no input queries.

locator.quote: so a single run happens to decide them

entry.feedback: Them grammatically refers to all three inputs, although a^- has no value under P and the experiment treats it exactly like a^+. The next paragraph corrects the reader, but this sentence briefly announces a decision that has not been defined.
entry.why_it_matters: The distinction between an accepted measurement outcome and a correct answer to the partial function is the lesson of the example.
entry.advice: Scope the sentence to the two promised examples, and describe the third as an accepted unpromised input. Retain the subsequent one-input with acceptance probability 1/4; it successfully prevents the examples from making the general decoder look exact.

locator.quote: and project onto $u$

entry.feedback: Projection is introduced as a verb without an operational interpretation. A mathematically literate reader may understand orthogonal projection of a vector but not that this is a two-outcome quantum measurement, with a success branch and its complementary branch.
entry.why_it_matters: The later sampler reuses success flags and conditioning on measurement; this is the earliest place to teach that operation concretely.
entry.advice: Identify the two possible measurement outcomes and derive the success probability as the squared inner product with u. For this small Walsh system, mention the equivalent inverse-Walsh-and-zero-outcome test if that is the representation the author wants to carry forward.

locator.quote: Of all $256$ inputs, $104$ are one-inputs, $48$ are zero-inputs and $104$ lie outside the promise

entry.feedback: The full census is exact but has no later use. It occurs immediately after the key quantum lesson, and the reader must decide whether these proportions matter to the hard distribution or to the acceptance algorithm. They do not: the later minimax distribution is a different object.
entry.why_it_matters: An unrelated count can look like evidence for an asymptotic lower bound that the next sentence correctly says this example cannot illustrate.
entry.advice: Put the census in the linked checking script or offer it as an optional exercise. Keep the L=0 limitation and the promise-versus-projection lesson in the main text.

locator.quote: We describe one column in general, then a four-column board.

entry.feedback: The section postpones the concrete column until after three input families, an addressed array, four winning conditions and two attribution paragraphs. At this stage the reader has only seen two sign vectors, not a circuit transcript or a pointer array.
entry.why_it_matters: The schema is easier to remember once the reader has watched one actual address select one actual cell.
entry.advice: Consider introducing the four-column layout first with only the fields needed to identify its winner, then name the general fields. Preserve the explicit statement that r=2 is a teaching simplification, which is already a successful repair from the previous round.

locator.quote: Column $i$ **wins** at address $s$ when four conditions hold

entry.feedback: The four clauses are compressed into one semicolon-separated paragraph, yet later passages refer to individual clauses and the Lean section asks the reader to inspect the second one. The clause structure is conceptually important but difficult to scan.
entry.why_it_matters: Readers cannot quickly compare a changed board against the definition or check that the local-test list covers every obligation.
entry.advice: Present the four genuinely parallel conditions as numbered clauses or a compact table, with the corresponding test family beside each. Keep the explanation of uniqueness immediately after them; it should not be separated from the pointer condition.

locator.quote: each reading one proposed gate value and the two values feeding it

entry.feedback: The previous-round plan SX-014 called for a pointer test and a gate test with their actual bit reads. The pointer test is now worked, but the gate test is still only described abstractly. All stored transcripts in the board are correct, so the reader never sees the local consistency check detect a false transcript.
entry.why_it_matters: The reason an arbitrary input can carry a useful certificate without trusting it remains asserted rather than demonstrated.
entry.advice: Use one existing gate from the linked 180-gate circuit, show its two predecessor values and proposed output, and flip only that output to show exactly which local equation fails. Keep the example tiny and use it to explain why a transcript is input data, not an oracle for circuit evaluation.

locator.quote: Shannon expansion of the truth tables gives such a circuit with $180$ gates

entry.feedback: Shannon expansion and the exact count 180 enter together without an explanation of either. The relevant point here is that a fixed public circuit exists and that a stored evaluation can be checked locally. The precise gate count is useful only for the later K=371 illustration.
entry.why_it_matters: The named construction sounds like an additional prerequisite at the point where the reader is learning the certificate mechanism.
entry.advice: Define the truth-table expansion in a short phrase if retained, or move its name to the linked circuit file. Make the role of 180 explicit: it supplies a concrete test count, not a new conceptual ingredient.

locator.quote: that cell certifies the answers

entry.feedback: The general-column picture emphasizes certifying address bits but does not visibly distinguish the domain checks from the value checks. The domain-bit counterexample immediately following the figure is one of the document’s central points.
entry.why_it_matters: A reader who recalls the diagram instead of the paragraph may remember only address agreement, precisely the insufficient condition the changed board refutes.
entry.advice: Add the domain-and-value distinction inside the cell’s short label or caption. The figure need not show the entire circuit; it should name the two kinds of conclusion its transcripts certify.

locator.quote: Column $1$ wins at $10$ (Figure 2); every other column has a zero in its own string, so $F=1$.

entry.feedback: The final so appears to make the zeros in the other columns the reason F=1. Those zeros show that the other columns cannot win; the positive value follows from column 1 satisfying all four conditions.
entry.why_it_matters: This is a small causal slip at the first complete evaluation of the new function.
entry.advice: Separate the positive conclusion from the uniqueness observation: first identify why column 1 passes, then use the zeros to exclude the others.

locator.quote: On the changed board, $(2,00)$ fails only its domain test

entry.feedback: This is an excellent exact instance of a single bad local test, but the exposition does not carry it into the quantum verifier later. With K=371, one uniform local test detects the error with probability 1/371; that is exactly why the verification uses amplitude amplification.
entry.why_it_matters: The circuit examples and the quantum subroutine remain separate lessons when they could explain one another.
entry.advice: Recall this same candidate in the Verification paragraph and use its one failing test to connect the stored-domain mistake to the threshold 1/K. Keep the exact Grover iteration calculation optional; the detection probability is the decisive bridge.

locator.quote: which of column $2$'s tests fail at each of its four addresses?

entry.feedback: This question tests a real distinction: a correct transcript can still fail the domain requirement, while an address mismatch contributes additional value-test failures. The answer is separate and can be checked directly from the data on the page.
entry.why_it_matters: It gives the reader an independent task tied to the actual total-function definition, rather than asking for a paraphrase of a theorem.
entry.advice: Keep it next to the changed board. If the four winning clauses are numbered, use the same numbering in the answer.

locator.quote: let $W_{ab}=(-1)^{a\cdot b}$, $H=W/\sqrt m$

entry.feedback: The dot product in the exponent is not specified as a binary dot product, and the text immediately uses H as a length-preserving operator. The four-by-four example verifies this once, but the general formula asks the reader to supply the Walsh orthogonality argument.
entry.why_it_matters: The norm bound on Phi and the legality of the quantum experiment both depend on this normalization.
entry.advice: Say that the exponent is computed modulo two, and identify H as the tensor product of the normalized two-by-two Hadamard transform. That supplies the relevant general fact without a separate proof excursion.

locator.quote: Repeating it $\rho=\lceil16c^{-1}\ln(1/\eta)\rceil$ times

entry.feedback: The parameter eta is first introduced inside the trial-count formula. The companion supplies the range 0<eta<1/2; the exposition does not name eta as the requested error tolerance before using it.
entry.why_it_matters: Later eta, epsilon and epsilon/r appear at different levels, and the reader needs their roles rather than three unexplained small quantities.
entry.advice: State the requested decoder error range before the formula, then name the later specialization eta=epsilon/r when decoding an address. Keep the distinction between per-bit error and per-address error explicit.

locator.quote: decides $P$ with error at most $\eta$

entry.feedback: The sentence ends with a query bound on every input, but correctness holds only on the promise. These are intentionally different scopes. Section 4 relies on the total running-time guarantee even for unpromised losers, while final verification handles the lack of a correct P-value there.
entry.why_it_matters: This split is the central obstacle in turning the partial function into a total one; it is too easy to lose inside a long sentence.
entry.advice: End the decoder paragraph by putting the two guarantees side by side in ordinary language: correctness on promised inputs; the same finite query cap on all inputs. This reinforces an existing argument rather than adding a warning or a new assumption.

locator.quote: Because $\Phi$ has two boundary factors and $k-1$ internal factors of $m^{-1/2}$

entry.feedback: The integer numerator, two threshold comparisons, ripple-carry arithmetic and the constant 200 receive one dense paragraph, but the reason the reader needs a nearly linear circuit is deferred. For this audience, the supplier’s role matters before its implementation details.
entry.why_it_matters: The reader can spend effort parsing arithmetic that never becomes an operation they perform, while missing why S controls the final quantum cost.
entry.advice: Lead with the consumed fact S=O_k(m log^2 m) and its consequence for the number of local tests. Put the exact integer derivation in an optional calculation or direct the reader to the existing record proof.

locator.quote: two boundary factors

entry.feedback: Boundary refers to the two u vectors, not to a boundary case of the promise. This terminology is never explained, and the following denominator 2^{t(k+1)} is the first expression that depends on counting those normalizations.
entry.why_it_matters: An elementary normalization count becomes harder to reconstruct than the displayed product itself.
entry.advice: If the integer calculation remains on the main route, identify the two u factors and the k−1 copies of H explicitly. This is a local naming repair, distinct from the recommendation about how much circuit arithmetic to retain.

locator.quote: which is $O_k(m^{22}(\log m)^3)$

entry.feedback: The large input length is presented as a formula and then immediately left behind. A reader may confuse m with the number of input bits or interpret the quartic separation as a running-time result in the full input length.
entry.why_it_matters: The comparison between R and Q is meaningful even though the addressed array is large, but the meaning of the complexity parameter must remain clear.
entry.advice: Attach one sentence distinguishing m from the total bit count n and explaining that the theorem compares the two query measures for the same large input family. Avoid suggesting practical end-to-end speedups from the query exponent alone.

locator.quote: The construction uses $k$-fold Forrelation through three facts

entry.feedback: This is the right abstraction boundary: low quantum cost, a small exact circuit, and classical hardness have different jobs. A reader can understand the total-function construction without reproducing the full Forrelation lower bound.
entry.why_it_matters: Keeping those jobs separate prevents the promise-solving algorithm from being mistaken for an exact domain checker.
entry.advice: Preserve the three-part interface. Add the downstream job to each label if revising the paragraph order: decode, verify, and force classical work.

locator.quote: Checking that one column wins means reading its $m$ string bits and following its $m-1$ pointers

entry.feedback: The sentence describes reading m bits and following m−1 pointers, then assigns that operation about sqrt(m) quantum queries. That is not what literally reading all those bits costs. The intended operation is bounded-error search for a violation among the local tests.
entry.why_it_matters: The first explanation of the quantum speedup can accidentally teach that a quantum algorithm reads a whole classical string in sqrt(m) queries.
entry.advice: Name the violation-search operation explicitly. Include transcript and output tests in the reference to K, then suppress logarithms for the intuitive sqrt(m) comparison. Preserve the useful warning that nesting this verification inside Grover over columns would lose the desired exponent.

locator.section: §4: nested search and the new mechanism
locator.quote: run the expensive check only on a short list of candidates

entry.feedback: This is the mechanism that turns the upper bound from roughly m into roughly sqrt(m), but the paragraph does not give the reader a compact view of the complete algorithm before the weight analysis starts. It is easy to mistake all the later weight updates for operations the computer executes.
entry.why_it_matters: The novel sampler is easier to assess when the operational stages are known in advance.
entry.advice: Give a short procedural outline: initialize the candidate list; use the coherent comparison preparation to sample another pivot; stop at a cap or reported failure; verify the accumulated candidates. Keep the ideal weights in a visibly separate analysis paragraph, as the text already says they are not computed.

locator.quote: Then we follow each decoded cell's pointer into the other column

entry.feedback: The pointer test in Section 2 reads one direction. The first comparison needs both directions, two decoded labels, a disqualification rule and a tie rule, but no full comparison is traced before the general probabilities a_ij are introduced.
entry.why_it_matters: The reader must mentally compose several earlier operations and can easily reverse which column a zero disqualifies.
entry.advice: Trace the existing pair 1 versus 2, showing the label returned for the unpromised a^- input, both pointer destinations, and the resulting victor. Make clear that the returned label in column 2 is not its true partial-function address.

locator.quote: Both orders of a pair run the same procedure
