entry.feedback: The companion explicitly sorts the two indices and runs one circuit for the unordered pair. Here same procedure could be read as two ordered calls whose roles or tie decisions are separately defined. The complement identity needs one common experiment with opposite outcome labels.
entry.why_it_matters: The exact identity a_ij+a_ji=1 is the entire drift argument’s algebraic input.
entry.advice: Retain the companion’s short implementation convention: normalize the unordered pair once and interpret the one outcome in the requested order. There is no need to add circuit machinery.

locator.section: §4: coherent implementation of the repeated decoder
locator.quote: Its trials, counts and decoded labels stay unmeasured in workspace

entry.feedback: Section 1 explicitly described a projection measurement and Section 3 repeated that experiment. This sentence now says those trials remain unmeasured. A newcomer needs the bridge from a measured probability calculation to a reversible circuit that records outcome bits without measuring them.
entry.why_it_matters: Otherwise the inverse used by amplitude amplification appears to undo a physical measurement, which it cannot do.
entry.advice: Explain that each would-be measurement result is retained in a flag register, the count and threshold are computed reversibly, and actual measurement is postponed. Keep the workspace through the inverse; do not describe it as already cleaned at this point.

locator.quote: and this is what makes $a_{ij}$ well defined

entry.feedback: The probability a_ij is well defined for any specified comparison measurement. Retaining labels establishes the stronger and relevant statement that the coherent comparison has the same output law as the decoded-label rule. The current ending understates that correspondence and suggests a definitional problem instead.
entry.why_it_matters: The reader should see why coherence preserves the specific probabilities used in the classical weight analysis.
entry.advice: End at equality of the two output laws. Preserve the explanation that orthogonal label branches contribute probabilities without cross terms.

locator.quote: Quantum minimum finding [@DH1996] needs a total order

entry.feedback: The quantum-side comparison jumps from minimum finding and bounded-error search directly to the present algorithm. The packet’s two 2026 comparison-based separations and king-finding paper appear in the bibliography but are never used in the exposition’s body. The companion identifies a more immediate set-to-weight relationship.
entry.why_it_matters: The reader may infer that comparison-based candidate generation followed by verification is itself the new contribution, rather than the treatment of arbitrarily biased loser comparisons.
entry.advice: Add a short, audience-appropriate comparison to the existing candidate-set and exact-orientation approaches, then identify the new fractional probabilities. Keep the distinction between certificate-complexity separation and randomized-query separation; do not import their theorems as if they already prove this result.

locator.quote: column $4$'s pointer into column $3$ names position $1$

entry.feedback: The three modified pointers are supplied in one long sentence, while the drawn edge labels mix the modified pointers with the unmodified pointers that actually certify each victory. The figure is correct, but checking one edge requires recovering both relevant pointer values from two sections.
entry.why_it_matters: The example intended to make nontransitivity immediate still demands bookkeeping before the cycle is visible.
entry.advice: Give a compact three-row comparison table listing the two target bits and the winner, or explicitly trace one edge and let the diagram carry the remaining two. Keep the current arrow convention and the fact that every cell is changed together.

locator.quote: so the decoders are exact and the comparisons deterministic

entry.feedback: The worked sampler deliberately makes every comparison deterministic. Consequently every weight is 0 or 1 and sampling by weight is just uniform sampling from surviving candidates. This illustrates cyclicity and measurement, but it never exhibits the fractional-weight feature that distinguishes the algorithm from set pruning. The previous round moved the fractional example out; the next-layer problem is that the surviving example no longer witnesses the novelty.
entry.why_it_matters: A reader can successfully run every exercise and still not understand why weights, exact conditional output laws and no margin from 1/2 matter.
entry.advice: Start from the existing abstract four-candidate example in record §5.2, which already gives unequal weights. To expose the arbitrary-loser feature as well, change one loser pair to a_ab=a_ba=1/2: after pivot a, the weights are (1−eps,0,1/2,1). Show their sum, success mass equal to that sum divided by four, and conditional pivot probabilities proportional to them. Label this as an abstract comparison-matrix variation, not an asserted realization by the addressed four-column board. No new theorem or bound is needed.

locator.quote: pairing the terms $w_iw_pa_{ip}$ and $w_pw_ia_{pi}$

entry.feedback: The pairing is the decisive elementary move, but the next display jumps directly to the full double sum. On a first reading it is easy to miss that the two pivot probabilities are already weighted, or that the diagonal terms vanish.
entry.why_it_matters: The elegant reason for the halving bound gets hidden behind notation even though it can be demonstrated in one pair.
entry.advice: Write one pair’s contribution as w_i w_p(a_ip+a_pi)=w_i w_p and explicitly remove i=p using a_ii=0. Then give the displayed full identity. Preserve the initial four-pivot table, which provides a useful numerical check.

locator.quote: Meanwhile the winner's weight stays at least $(1-\varepsilon)^T

entry.feedback: The preceding paragraph bounds expected total weight, while this one bounds the winner’s weight on each history before selection. That change in logical strength is essential to the missing-winner event inclusion but is not named.
entry.why_it_matters: A student may think both statements are expectations and fail to see why a small expected total forces the winner to have been selected.
entry.advice: Say that the lower bound holds on every unselected-winner history, then connect that pathwise fact to the expectation bound. The current Markov calculation can remain unchanged.

locator.quote: Suppose pivots $p_1,\dots,p_j$ have been chosen.

entry.feedback: The preparation is described only with an existing pivot list. The initial empty-history case is what starts the actual algorithm and makes the ideal first-pivot table relevant, but its empty-product convention is never stated.
entry.why_it_matters: The process can appear to require a pivot before it knows how to obtain one.
entry.advice: Add that with no previous pivots every branch has success flag 1 and the first measured pivot is uniform over columns. It requires no comparisons. This is a useful operational base case, not a new analysis.

locator.section: §4: good state at zero success probability
locator.quote: let $g$ be the normalised state on its success branch

entry.feedback: This definition needs p>0, while the same paragraph later emphasizes the p=0 case. The expert lemma correctly limits the normalized successful state to p>0. There is no normalized success branch at p=0.
entry.why_it_matters: The exposition’s most important all-input endpoint is being described with an object undefined there.
entry.advice: Copy the short p>0 qualification from the companion, and handle p=0 separately through certain failure. This is a statement clarification, not a gap in the intended bounded-amplification argument.

locator.quote: the state is exactly $g$, whatever the number of iterations

entry.feedback: The successful amplitude sin((2j+1)theta) can be negative, so the normalized vector can be -g. The companion correctly says up to a global phase. The measurable conclusion needed here, preservation of the conditional column distribution, is unaffected.
entry.why_it_matters: The word exactly creates an unnecessary discrepancy between the two funnel documents at the place where state versus output-law distinctions matter.
entry.advice: Use the companion’s global-phase qualification or state only the invariant conditional label law. Do not expand the exposition into a discussion of formal vector representatives.

locator.section: §4: standard amplification proof dominates the route
locator.quote: Either way a trial succeeds with probability at least $9/40$.

entry.feedback: The current paragraph retains M=ceil(10/sqrt(gamma)), the 3/4 case split, 19/40, 9/40 and ln(40/31). Round-six SX-022, QX-020 and CX024 explicitly planned to move this recipe to the record while retaining the interface. The delivered paragraph is still a full unboxed standard proof, occupying the bottom of page 8 and spilling onto page 9.
entry.why_it_matters: The newcomer must absorb constant-level amplification arithmetic immediately before the construction-specific sampler example, while the genuinely new fractional behavior has been removed.
entry.advice: Implement the already accepted weighting decision: keep the fixed cap, unknown-p guarantee, certain failure at p=0 and preservation of the successful label distribution. Route the trial recipe and constants to record §5.1 or a clearly optional box.

locator.section: §4: coupling without a new probability prerequisite
locator.quote: Coupling the real and ideal processes until the first failure

entry.feedback: Coupling is used as a technical verb without being defined. The preceding exact conditional law makes a very short explanation possible: as long as the histories agree and the real sampler succeeds, use the same pivot in both processes.
entry.why_it_matters: The reader may treat the T epsilon term as a mysterious theorem or assume it requires independent stage failures.
entry.advice: Give that common-pivot construction in a sentence and state that the per-history failure bound is enough for the union bound. Preserve the existing restriction to stages before the winner is listed.

locator.quote: Decoding errors inside comparisons are already part of the $a_{ij}$.

entry.feedback: This short closing sentence explains why the analysis does not charge a decoder error for every one of the many coherent comparison calls. That is a major conceptual difference from a naive replacement of noisy comparisons by a perfect orientation, but it appears only after the full error budget.
entry.why_it_matters: A quantum-trained reader may incorrectly expect the decoder accuracy to scale inversely with all amplified oracle uses and misunderstand the reason the tournament works.
entry.advice: Promote this explanation to the point where a_ij is introduced or where the sampler is amplified. Explain that amplitude amplification manipulates the actual coherent comparison, whose output probabilities define the weights; the analysis never posits a globally correct hidden tournament.

locator.quote: amplify over the $K$ local tests

entry.feedback: The local tests were described as adaptive classical bit reads, including following a pointer. The verifier now uses them in a coherent search without stating the implementation bridge that the companion supplies: a reversible controlled test-index evaluator and its inverse.
entry.why_it_matters: The reader can wonder whether following all possible pointers in superposition assumes an extra memory-access primitive or makes the cost exponential in the array size.
entry.advice: Explain that a local test computes its next bit address reversibly, uses the same bit oracle, and retains enough workspace to invert the computation, with a constant-factor query overhead. Link to the existing coherent-test argument for details.

locator.section: §4: actual query counts versus fixed caps
locator.quote: Every number of trials, iterations, stages and comparisons is fixed in advance

entry.feedback: This is false as a description of the algorithm just given. A trial randomly chooses its number of Grover iterations; the amplification procedure stops at its first success; the tournament stops on reported failure; and a stage uses the number of pivots already obtained. The actual counts therefore vary between branches. The proof needs and has fixed upper bounds on those counts, not fixed realized counts.
entry.why_it_matters: The sentence conflates a bounded adaptive algorithm with a fixed-length execution and weakens the explanation of the worst-case query convention.
entry.advice: Replace the claim about fixed numbers by a claim about input-independent caps on every branch. Preserve early stopping and randomized iteration counts. The asymptotic upper bound does not need to change. The preprint §3.2 already uses fixed upper bounds rather than fixed realized counts; align this sentence with it.

locator.quote: A comparison costs $c=O_k(r\log(r/\varepsilon))$ queries

entry.feedback: The symbol c previously meant the small probability delta^2 in Section 3; here it becomes a growing query cost. Neither use is wrong locally, but both reappear in the amplitude-amplification discussion and the reader is not told that the symbol has been repurposed.
entry.why_it_matters: A reader checking the cost chain can inadvertently carry the probability c into the comparison-count formula.
entry.advice: Use a descriptive cost symbol or state the cost without assigning c in the exposition. The companion may retain its compact specialist notation.

locator.quote: This is the $\sqrt m$ half of the arithmetic in the introduction.

entry.feedback: The section returns to the exact quantity that motivated it, after distinguishing candidate generation from expensive verification. This closure is useful: it tells the reader which part of the theorem has now been supplied.
entry.why_it_matters: A long algorithmic derivation otherwise risks losing the global separation argument.
entry.advice: Keep this closing connection. If the standard amplification constants move out, use the recovered space to explain the fractional sampler rather than to expand the query-count algebra.

locator.quote: and leave every cell blank

entry.feedback: Blank is an evocative diagram label, but the input was defined as an assignment of Boolean bits. The companion specifies that every cell bit is zero. Here blank can sound like absent data or a special symbol outside the input alphabet.
entry.why_it_matters: The simulator must answer every queried cell bit, and its answer is what makes the dummy transcript independent of the planted column.
entry.advice: Say once that blank means all bits are zero. Keep the visual blank-cell notation after that definition.

locator.section: §5: what the small example cannot prove
locator.quote: At $m=4$ there is no hard distribution

entry.feedback: As written this is too strong. Section 1 gives L_{2,4}=0. A distribution assigning probability 1/2 each to the promised inputs a^+ and a^0 makes every zero-query algorithm correct with probability at most 1/2, hence meets the displayed at-most-2/3 hardness condition at this L. What fails at m=4 is a useful positive query budget and the later division by L, not the existence of any hard distribution.
entry.why_it_matters: The caveat intended to prevent overclaiming introduces a false mathematical statement and obscures exactly which hypothesis the teaching board lacks.
entry.advice: Say that the asymptotic hardness bound supplies no positive L at this size, so the picture illustrates the two places where inputs differ only. Retain the explicit reset of address inputs and cell contents introduced in the last revision. This is a local caveat correction; the main asymptotic theorem is unaffected.

locator.quote: condition on the whole transcript of the dummy run

entry.feedback: The query-by-query discovery probability must be conditioned on the history so far, before the next query. Whole transcript can mean the completed run, which can already reveal whether a particular discovery occurred. The companion says given the past. The round-six repair correctly added independence of the other fields but left this temporal ambiguity.
entry.why_it_matters: The same adaptive-conditioning discipline is used again in the direct-product proof, so a loose statement here teaches the wrong filtration.
entry.advice: Say the entire observed history up to the current query, together with the fact that the current column’s zero has not yet been found. Then give the residual uniformity and 2/m bound. Do not claim the next discovery remains random after conditioning on its future answer.

locator.section: §5: why the classical gap is at least one third
locator.quote: A randomized algorithm computing $F$ with $G$ queries would have gap at least $1/3$

entry.feedback: The concluding discrepancy contradiction is compact enough that the reader has to reconstruct the direction of both error inequalities. The construction of the pair is explicit, but the final link back to the definition of R is not written.
entry.why_it_matters: This is where the lower-bound argument becomes a statement about every bounded-error algorithm, rather than only the selected dummy and planted distributions.
entry.advice: Write the two inequalities for acceptance on Y^1 and Y^0, namely at least 2/3 and at most 1/3, before subtracting. The subsequent averaging over deterministic trees then has a visible target.

locator.section: §5: explaining the simulator as an address predictor
locator.quote: outputs $s$, read off from the position of that query without reading the cell

entry.feedback: This is the clearest formulation of the lower-bound mechanism. It tells the reader why merely guessing or visiting cells still constitutes a simultaneous prediction of the address bits, without claiming that an algorithm must explicitly compute the address first.
entry.why_it_matters: The position-versus-content distinction is what makes the direct-product theorem apply to arbitrary adaptive algorithms.
entry.advice: Keep this sentence and the total-cap-to-separate-caps explanation. Do not shorten them back into a slogan that reaching a cell requires first learning its address.

locator.quote: $k=2$ gives exactly the cube.

entry.feedback: The word exactly is too strong for the bounds being used. At k=2 the leading powers match a cubic comparison, but the lower-bound and upper-bound logarithms remain. The companion correctly says fixed k excludes exponents strictly below 4−2/k and does not provide an exact quartic separation.
entry.why_it_matters: The phrase can undo the careful strict-exponent and logarithmic-loss discussion in the surrounding paragraph.
entry.advice: Say that k=2 gives the cubic exponent at the level of the leading powers and does not refute the cubic bound. Keep k=3 as the concrete parameter that does refute it.

locator.quote: $k=4$ gives exactly $3.5$ and does not suffice

entry.feedback: The answer conflates proving alpha_tot at least 3.5 with refuting a universal bound of exponent exactly 3.5. The question asks for the former. Fixed k=4 does suffice for that conclusion: for every alpha<3.5, d=2−1/4−alpha/2>0, so the displayed ratio diverges and no smaller exponent works. The same bounds do not establish divergence at alpha=3.5 itself; choosing k=5 does that stronger job.
entry.why_it_matters: The exercise intended to teach strict inequalities instead teaches an incorrect implication about an infimum.
entry.advice: Either change the question’s objective to ruling out R≤C(1+Q)^{3.5}, for which the given k=5 answer fits the argument, or say k=4 suffices for alpha_tot≥3.5 while k=5 excludes the endpoint bound. The main alpha_tot=4 proof is unaffected.

locator.section: §6: the fixed-parameter route and the companion
locator.quote: a $k$ that grows with $m$ cannot be substituted into these bounds

entry.feedback: The qualification these bounds is correct, but a reader following the companion finds a later uniform-in-k estimate and a diagonal choice. The two documents can look contradictory unless the distinction between the fixed-k theorem used here and the stronger uniform input used there is made navigable.
entry.why_it_matters: The funnel should make clear which extra estimate permits a different parameter choice, without making the exposition carry that proof.
entry.advice: Add a short pointer saying that a growing-k construction requires additional uniform estimates, treated in the companion and record. Keep the present fixed-k proof as the exposition’s main route and keep the t≥2^k counterexample.

locator.quote: the record reconstructs it with the constant $35^4$

entry.feedback: The constant 35^4 appears only in a final parenthesis and plays no role in why four is optimal. A newcomer has just completed the separation argument and is now asked to notice a numerical refinement of a theorem being imported.
entry.why_it_matters: The ending shifts attention from the achieved conceptual payoff to an unused constant.
entry.advice: Keep the citation and full-proof link for the universal quartic bound, but leave this constant to the record or companion unless a later use needs it.

locator.quote: There [$R$][def-R] is defined through [finite random mixtures][def-randomized] of [decision trees][def-tree]

entry.feedback: The formal-verification section is much more appropriate after the last revision, but its first paragraph still contains a dense run of linked definitions and theorem variants. The genuinely useful novice entry, checking the winning condition on the changed board, comes only in the next paragraph.
entry.why_it_matters: A reader looking for one meaningful formal check can mistake the link cluster for a required tour of the implementation vocabulary.
entry.advice: Lead with the changed-board check and retain one link to the full statement file. Let the model-definition links be an optional second route. Preserve the plain statement of the one material difference, the unspecified logarithmic power, without adding receipt or review-status prose.

locator.section: Answers and exercises: what understanding is tested
locator.quote: What does one Grover iteration do here?

entry.feedback: The four questions test local winning clauses, a deterministic next pivot, an independence calculation and a parameter inequality. None tests the new sampler’s unequal conditional distribution or asks the reader to distinguish a sampler failure from evidence that no winner exists. The current second question happens to end with a single surviving column and success after one Grover iteration.
entry.why_it_matters: A student can answer all four questions while still treating the quantum algorithm as ordinary elimination with a magical speedup.
entry.advice: Retarget or supplement Question 2 using the record’s abstract fractional example, with one loser pair set to probability 1/2 so that a genuinely fractional loser weight remains after the first pivot. Ask for the joint success masses and conditional pivot probabilities, or ask what a failure after listing the winner changes. State the abstract comparison-matrix scope explicitly.

locator.quote: A column that dominates the comparisons is therefore only a candidate

entry.feedback: The changed pointer demonstrates a precise failure mode: comparison dominance alone does not certify a positive input. It motivates final verification using an actual malformed total-function input, rather than a warning detached from the construction.
entry.why_it_matters: This is a robust teaching example that survives changes in the presentation of the sampler.
entry.advice: Keep it before the algorithm’s correctness analysis, and return to its single failed pointer test when explaining verification. Its role differs from the domain-bit example and from the loser cycle.

locator.section: §4: the algorithm does not know its analytical weights
locator.quote: The weights are defined from the unknown probabilities $a_{ij}$; the algorithm never computes or estimates them.

entry.feedback: This sentence prevents the most damaging operational misreading of the proof. The following sampler computes with coherent comparisons; the weights are quantities used to prove its distribution and progress.
entry.why_it_matters: Without it, the claimed speedup can seem to assume free access to an m-by-m table of probabilities.
entry.advice: Keep this sentence at the first introduction of weights and retain the exact success-and-column mass formula as its constructive explanation.

locator.quote: stopping cannot remove a listed column

entry.feedback: This is the right explanation of the asymmetric failure analysis. The sampler can have tiny success mass after the winner is already listed; correctness depends on retaining the list, not on successfully completing every possible stage.
entry.why_it_matters: It protects the all-input bounded-time algorithm from being confused with an unbounded search guaranteed to find another pivot.
entry.advice: Keep the statement beside the stopping rule. If the coupling paragraph is shortened, preserve this temporal condition explicitly.

locator.quote: yet substituting $k=t$ asks for $t\ge2^t$, which never holds.

entry.feedback: This elementary example makes a genuine quantifier-order error visible without importing more of the Forrelation proof. It is short, memorable and directly relevant to the temptation to set k as a function of m.
entry.why_it_matters: An otherwise formal warning becomes an inference the intended reader can test independently.
entry.advice: Keep it, while qualifying the neighboring statement to the fixed-k bounds actually used in this exposition. The companion’s uniform route can remain a linked extension.

entry.problem: The delivered rule set is incomplete relative to its own description and detector references. The stage description promises twenty-six general rules. Both supplied rule representations contain seventeen: RG-03, RG-04, RG-05, RG-07, RG-08, RG-10, RG-12, RG-23 and RG-25 are absent. The measurement still refers to several of these. A reviewer cannot assess the announced method from this packet.

instances.quote: Twenty-six general rules form one writing method.

instances.detail: The detector refers to missing RG-10 and RG-25.

entry.existing_safeguard: The method validates rule IDs and scopes and says the packet carries the method into every review.
entry.what_to_do_instead: When preparing a review copy, preserve the complete set of rule bodies and IDs. Remove private specimens or history fields individually, and disclose that those fields were omitted. Validate that every advertised rule and every detector rule reference resolves in the exported copy. This is an export-integrity repair, not a reason to add material to any paper.
entry.acceptance_check: A reviewer can locate all advertised rules, and every rule ID printed beside a measurement resolves to a supplied rule body.

entry.problem: The qualitative instruction selects literature close in genre, but the reported quantitative comparison applies the same forty-two-document corpus to a short specialist companion, a teaching article and a long reference record. The resulting distances combine differences of purpose with weaknesses of writing. The record's appendix apparatus and the exposition's questions have legitimate functions that a research-paper median does not represent.

instances.detail: Each uses 'cited literature (n=42 documents)'. The record apparatus score and the exposition question score are compared with the same baseline.

instances.quote: The record can be read along four routes.

entry.existing_safeguard: RG-01 explicitly says to choose the closest sources in genre, and the profiler is a detector rather than a gate.
entry.what_to_do_instead: Make that genre choice affect the report itself. Show comparisons with a small named set of relevant research papers for the expert companion, teaching sources for the exposition, and extended proofs or reference works for the record. Separate the record's mathematical body from its evidence appendices before discussing apparatus. Keep the broad corpus as background rather than as a target distribution.
entry.acceptance_check: Every recommended prose edit names the reader benefit; none is justified merely by moving a feature toward the all-literature median.

entry.problem: The extracted spans are not consistently the prose a reader sees. The expert report lists YAML front matter as a specimen for paragraph-length variation; mathematical expressions are collapsed to MATH and citations to placeholders. These transformations can alter segmentation and apparent cadence. The current report is therefore useful for locating paragraphs, but its numerical distances are not a clean measurement of rendered prose quality.

instances.detail: The first specimen begins at L1 with the YAML title, subtitle, author, date, bibliography and link-citations fields.
Displayed mathematics is represented by MATH inside the measured sentence stream.

entry.existing_safeguard: The method says the reviewer must read every candidate in its source.
entry.what_to_do_instead: Make the extraction assumptions visible beside the report, and exclude metadata that is not rendered as prose. Compare like extraction formats and inspect the source and reading copy before interpreting a segmentation-based statistic. Preserve equations as boundaries even when their tokens are excluded from prose counts.
entry.acceptance_check: The report can explain why its sampled paragraphs correspond to paragraphs a reader actually encounters; obvious metadata never becomes a sentence-level editing target.

entry.problem: Several leading detector hits are mathematically necessary or bibliographic. Author lists are classified as rhetorical triads, 'record' in a useful proof destination contributes to status vocabulary, and 'exactly' can state equality rather than emphasis. The large status score persists even though both short papers have apparatus_rate zero. An editing pass that follows the leading hits mechanically will remove credit, qualifications or navigation.

instances.detail: Examples include Aaronson, Ben-David and Kothari; Göös, Pitassi and Watson; and Ambainis, Iraids and Kokainis.

instances.quote: the column has exactly the ideal pivot law
No order or transitivity enters, so cycles among losers do no harm.

entry.existing_safeguard: The rules already distinguish mathematical negation from rhetoric and genuine lists from cadence.
entry.what_to_do_instead: Classify each proposed edit by the function of the flagged words before editing: mathematical assertion, attribution, necessary navigation or empty rhetoric. Record a scoped preservation reason for the first three. Prioritize repeated argument structure or overloaded paragraphs over harmless surface matches.
entry.acceptance_check: The revision retains exactness where the proof needs it and credits every source even if the corresponding detector score stays high.

entry.problem: The demand to improve every sentence is productive as a demand to reconsider it, but it becomes hazardous if interpreted as a demand to alter it. The preceding round records 501 line edits in the record and forty-four subsequent corrections after an independent audit. That history shows that mathematical invariants need protection at the moment of editing, not only after a large batch. It does not establish that every remaining sentence needs changing.

instances.quote: There is always something to improve in a sentence

instances.detail: The execution note reports 501 edits, of which 44 were corrected after an independent audit.

entry.existing_safeguard: RG-02 already permits an unchanged paragraph with a stated reason and forbids mathematical changes in the prose pass.
entry.what_to_do_instead: Keep the whole-document reread, but treat preservation as a real editorial outcome. Before changing a difficult paragraph, name its active objects, quantifier order, conditioning event, resource guarantee and credit. Recheck those specific invariants immediately after the edit. Group edits around a reader problem, not around a quota of changed sentences.
entry.acceptance_check: An improved paragraph is easier to follow while making the same assertions about the same procedure and event; a clear paragraph may remain unchanged for a concrete reason.

entry.problem: RG-16's preferred positive specimen, 'the argument uses only the law of the measured label', is now too underspecified to serve as an unconditional replacement template. The current expert formalisation paragraph carefully names a procedure that measures the label and resets the workspace; the record separately proves a successful-state assertion. Replacing that distinction with the specimen could reintroduce the earlier scope confusion. This is a stale method example, not a request to reopen the repaired formal claims.

instances.quote: the argument uses only the law of the measured label
a procedure that measures the label and resets its workspace
This is a statement about a designated subsystem

entry.existing_safeguard: The method already says equality of endpoints does not identify states, operations or proof routes.
entry.what_to_do_instead: Make positive rewriting preserve the subject of the claim. State which procedure has which output law and what subsequent operation uses it. Retain one precise negative distinction whenever it prevents an invalid substitution. Refresh illustrative method examples after a substantive correction, rather than leaving the old compression as a recommended model.
entry.acceptance_check: A reader can identify the procedure and permissible continuation from the shortened sentence without importing properties from a different implementation.

rule_or_skill: skills/long-to-short/SKILL.md: Model the reader and find the one point
entry.problem: Several individually reasonable opening obligations accumulate into an opening that is harder than its central idea. The expert companion's contribution paragraph introduces four constants, a threshold, a fixed-circuit requirement, a direct-product observation, a tournament relation, a uniform bound, a growing-parameter family and formalisation. Its intended reader still needs a compact reason that this construction beats the earlier cubic recipe. The existing instruction to rank obligations when the page budget is exceeded has not visibly governed the paragraph.

instances.quote: This paper adds the following to the preprint.
The quantum search needs care.

entry.existing_safeguard: The short-paper skill explicitly prioritizes the reader's next decision and the decisive mechanism over accumulated obligations.
entry.what_to_do_instead: After assembling required opening material, perform a second selection by function: what the reader must know to understand the result now, what establishes credit, and what matters only when checking a bound later. Keep the mechanism and contribution visible; move exact engineering constants to their first use or a compact later statement. Do this by replacement and relocation, not by adding an extra overview paragraph.
entry.acceptance_check: After the opening, an expert can state both the earlier obstruction and the operation that changes its cost without recalling the numerical constants.

rule_or_skill: skills/long-to-short/SKILL.md: comparison with the closest prior work
entry.problem: A bibliography of adjacent techniques can look like a novelty argument without exposing the actual point of non-applicability. Here minimum finding, fixed-tournament king finding, search on bounded-error bits, exact local comparisons and approximate fixed-edge oracles have different input contracts. Saying only that each is a tournament or a search loses the distinction that matters: a losing pair may have no orientation computable with a uniform bounded-error guarantee.

instances.quote: in each a comparison has a fixed intended outcome
Their classical measure is certificate complexity

entry.existing_safeguard: The skills already require comparison by hypotheses, conclusions, quantitative loss and the application's parameters.
entry.what_to_do_instead: For the closest antecedents, compare the oracle supplied, the promised correctness event, the returned object and the charged resource. Identify exactly which missing premise prevents a direct invocation. Use a small table only when those axes are genuinely independent. Do not infer impossibility for an entire framework from the limitations of one recipe, and do not call a standard cap conversion novel merely because it is made explicit here.
entry.acceptance_check: The reader can say why the named theorem does or does not apply, without relying on the authors' assertion that the methods differ.

entry.problem: The method already forbids repairing a teaching failure by silently raising prerequisites, but the current exposition places substantial quantum and complexity prerequisites at the entrance. A reader's ability to recognize the phrase 'amplitude amplification' is different from their ability to recover a conditional output law from retained work registers. Declaring the former does not discharge the latter.

instances.quote: branches with different labels stay orthogonal and cannot interfere
The comparisons then act on separate fresh registers

entry.existing_safeguard: The exposition skill explicitly distinguishes an operation a reader can perform from a list of named prerequisites, and says a narrower audience changes the requested scope.
entry.what_to_do_instead: Enforce the existing operation-level test at the two or three decisive uses. Ask the intended reader to predict a branch probability, identify which register is measured, and explain what is available to the next stage. If the passage does not supply that ability, repair it locally with an already supported small calculation. Do not solve the problem by expanding the prerequisite list.
entry.acceptance_check: The promised audience can perform the needed operation at its first consequential use; the review states whether this was an author simulation or an actual reader attempt.

rule_or_skill: skills/record-to-expository/SKILL.md: changed cases and distinguishing examples
entry.problem: An example can satisfy the theorem and still hide the new feature. The exposition's cyclic board is excellent for defeating a total-order interpretation, but its decoder outcomes and comparisons are deterministic. The record's four-candidate example gives nonuniform fractional weights through the nearly perfect distinguished row, while the loser-to-loser edges remain certain. Neither local example directly makes the reader work with a losing pair near one half, which is the distinction used against bounded-error fixed-predicate search.

instances.quote: the decoders are exact and the comparisons deterministic
these three certain comparisons are inconsistent with every total ordering

entry.existing_safeguard: The skills already require examples that separate operations the reader might identify, and a changed case when an easy example hides the needed distinction.
entry.what_to_do_instead: After selecting the teaching example, list the false inferences it blocks and the ones it leaves intact. Preserve the existing deterministic cycle for its clear purpose. Where fractional comparisons carry the new argument, use a brief abstract comparison-table variation or the record's nonuniform sampler calculation, explicitly distinguishing an abstract tournament example from a construction of the full input. The recommendation is explanatory reuse of the existing theorem, not a new theorem or an unverified realizability claim.
entry.acceptance_check: The reader can separately explain why cycles defeat sorting and why a comparison near one half is outside a uniform bounded-error orientation oracle.

rule_or_skill: skills/record-to-expository/SKILL.md: proof detail by reader use
entry.problem: A mathematically necessary guarantee is repeatedly treated as though every numerical detail of its proof belongs in every genre. The exposition carries the full 19/40, 9/40 and logarithmic trial-count calculation before resuming the candidate search. This is a place where the current draft still spends the reader's attention on a standard amplification constant instead of the distinctive conditional sampling law. The prior round already identified this allocation problem; the issue is that the revision did not enforce the intended allocation.

instances.quote: Either way a trial succeeds with probability at least $9/40$.
conditional on success its output state is $|g\rangle$ up to a global phase

entry.existing_safeguard: The method requires placing known background according to the audience's needs and preserving complete destinations for compressed proofs.
entry.what_to_do_instead: Decide separately whether the reader needs the contract, the reason for the contract, and the exact constant. Keep the fixed all-input cap, the zero-success case and the preserved conditional law at the call site. Give the direct-trial idea where it explains the high-success boundary. Route the numerical averaging bound to the record when it does not advance the exposition's promised task.
entry.acceptance_check: The exposition reader can explain why the search terminates and why it samples the intended pivot; the exact constant remains available without interrupting that explanation.

entry.problem: Dependency order alone does not tell the reader what the algorithm actually does. The tournament proof has an ideal weighted process, a reversible preparation, a measured pivot history, an amplified trial and a separate verifier. All are necessary, but the central distinction is which quantities exist only in the proof and which values the algorithm has learned. The current exposition's sentence that the algorithm never computes the weights is a particularly good repair and should become the model for other adaptive constructions.

instances.quote: the algorithm never computes or estimates them
the outcome becomes the next pivot, a classical value that later preparations use
Fix the current classical pivot list

entry.existing_safeguard: The skills require explicit operations and the order of dependent choices.
entry.what_to_do_instead: At each adaptive transition, state what is fixed, what is sampled, what is retained coherently, what is measured, and what is known at the next step. Keep this in the mathematical narrative; it need not become a repeated five-field checklist. Use proof-only variables to explain a calculation only after making their unavailability to the algorithm clear.
entry.acceptance_check: A reader can narrate one actual run without pretending the algorithm knows a probability or weight used only in the analysis.

entry.problem: Compression can move a premise after the formula it qualifies. The expert account introduces a general partial function g, displays a quantum cost without Q(g), and only then assumes Q(g) is polylogarithmic. The conclusion intended for the earlier AND–OR recipe is sound under that assumption; the trouble is the order in which the reader receives it. The cited cheat-sheet source places its small-Q(g) assumption before deriving the cost.

instances.quote: In their construction a partial function $g$ on $n$ bits is composed
If $Q(g)$ is polylogarithmic

entry.existing_safeguard: The skills already require hypotheses beside the inference they support and quantitative comparison with the application at hand.
entry.what_to_do_instead: When compressing a source calculation, check every displayed expression against only the premises already introduced. Either announce the restriction before the display or retain the parameter in the displayed formula. More generally, preserve the source's logical order even when changing its narrative order.
entry.acceptance_check: A reader stopping at the formula has already been given all hypotheses needed to read it as stated.
entry.outside_source: Aaronson, Ben-David and Kothari, Separations in query complexity using cheat sheets, arXiv:1511.01937v2, §3.1, printed pp. 9–10; https://arxiv.org/pdf/1511.01937

entry.problem: An existing destination is not necessarily the correct destination. The record's ideal tournament paragraph sends the reader back to §4.2 of the specialist companion, but the current companion's tournament is §3.2. This is a reader-route failure that a file-exists or anchor-exists check cannot detect. The underlying arguments and formal evidence need not be reopened to fix it.

instances.quote: Return to the [specialist companion](expert_companion.md), §4.2.

entry.existing_safeguard: The short-paper skill already requires following a full journey and verifying the argument at the destination.
entry.what_to_do_instead: Test the semantic arrival: the named section must begin or contain the inference the link promises, with enough local context to resume. After section reordering, check incoming return pointers as well as outgoing references. Keep locators readable and resolve the ordinary mathematical task, not only the URL.
entry.acceptance_check: Following the pointer puts the reader at the intended argument, and the return lands at the step that needed it.

rule_or_skill: skills/long-to-short/SKILL.md: title, abstract and proof coverage
entry.problem: The opening promise of a complete argument is stronger in the reader's ear than the later inventory of imported facts. The expert companion says it gives the complete argument, then explains that it cites Forrelation hardness, circuit properties, local tests, amplification facts, minimax and the universal bound. This may be a defensible mathematical convention for a specialist paper, but the method should check that the particular audience understands its scope before rewarding the phrase as a contribution.

instances.quote: We give the complete argument with explicit constants
We cite, and do not reprove

entry.existing_safeguard: The skill requires an intelligible proof or an explicitly labelled sketch, with all omitted inferences assigned destinations.
entry.what_to_do_instead: Define the scope of a completeness claim by its mathematical task: a complete derivation of the total-function separation from specified inputs, for example. Keep the imported-input inventory brief and useful, and align the abstract's promise with it. Avoid increasing the paper with proofs its audience already accepts merely to preserve an expansive adjective.
entry.acceptance_check: The reader knows what they can verify within this paper and which named results they are being asked to accept, before they invest in the proof.

entry.problem: Several rules are sound as judgments but risky as surface transformations. Breaking a three-item list into two or four items has no intrinsic explanatory benefit; mathematical comparisons sometimes need a negative sentence; a single organisation formula from the literature is not a universal opening template. The current papers need variation of argument and reader load more than cosmetic variation in list length.

instances.quote: Break rule-of-three lists into two items, four named objects or a full clause.
The definition imposes no promise on the address inputs, pointers or transcripts

entry.existing_safeguard: RG-19 already permits genuinely parallel named triples; RG-17 permits mathematical negation and actual comparisons.
entry.what_to_do_instead: Phrase the editorial decision in terms of the defect: redundant items, vague category names, parallel sentences that do different jobs, or rhetoric that hides the positive claim. Preserve a natural three-part mathematical inventory when it expresses three real objects. Treat punctuation and count restrictions as author preferences, never evidence that a mathematical passage is clear.
entry.acceptance_check: Each surface change has an identifiable semantic or reading benefit, and no artificial fourth item is introduced to satisfy a cadence detector.

entry.problem: Freshness has two distinct jobs: locating new relevant work and verifying the edition actually used. A newer version is not itself evidence that an older comparison is wrong. The supplied AIK paper is v2, while a public v3 is available; the fixed-graph and capped-search mechanisms relevant here already occur in the supplied version. A new tournament-solutions paper was discovered online, but its primary body was inaccessible in this review. Neither observation licenses a novelty objection from a title or abstract.

instances.quote: [AIK2026, arXiv v2]

instances.detail: The supplied version specifies the fixed underlying graph, U(W), approximate edge routines and a capped FindSource procedure.

entry.existing_safeguard: The method already distinguishes an unavailable source from a source inspected and found insufficient.
entry.what_to_do_instead: Record the inspected edition and exact source scope. Search for recent work, then compare the actual relevant theorem or algorithm before changing a novelty statement. Treat abstract-only discoveries as leads. Update a citation only when its content, metadata or locator needs updating; do not turn version age into a defect by itself.
entry.acceptance_check: Every substantive comparison is supported by a read primary passage, and the review makes unavailable bodies and sampled newer editions explicit.

entry.problem: Finding a move in three research literatures supports its plausibility and scope; it does not show that readers understand a new manuscript better because of it. The register-stage account correctly labels candidates, but the phrase 'tested in three fields' can be overread as an outcome evaluation. The same danger applies when an AI reviewer successfully follows a proof after consulting the record and then reports that the first encounter teaches it well.

instances.quote: Each general rule was then tested against the cited literature
Judge by what a reader can do.

entry.existing_safeguard: The exposition skill already separates author checks from actual reader responses and says a checked example is not evidence of understanding.
entry.what_to_do_instead: Name the evidence precisely: corpus occurrence, editorial judgment, simulated first read, or observed reader reconstruction. Use a bounded task to evaluate a proposed change, such as recovering the invariant after a changed case. Report the result only if that task was actually attempted; leave human-reader validation unperformed when no person participated.
entry.acceptance_check: No claimed teaching success rests solely on publication style, a detector score, a working link, or the reviewer's assisted reread.

entry.problem: The method contains a useful tension that needs an explicit decision rule. RG-06 says a long record replaces a reading guide with an organisation paragraph, while RG-21 allows a short guide for required and optional routes. This record has several materially different tasks, so its route table is justified. The remaining issue is repeated orientation and invariant recitals inside the proof, not the mere presence of a guide.

instances.quote: a long record replaces a reading guide with this paragraph
The long record may keep a short reading guide
We first fix the comparison model and the parameters.

entry.existing_safeguard: The long-record skill already distinguishes logical dependency order from the best reading order and allows independent entry points.
entry.what_to_do_instead: Choose the navigation device by the number of genuinely different reader tasks. Use one concise route guide when the document supports several; use one prose organisation paragraph for a largely sequential paper. At a local entry repeat only the objects needed to recover the omitted inference, and remove repeated statements of the entire programme.
entry.acceptance_check: The reader can choose a route once, then follow the mathematics without repeated instructions to choose again.

entry.problem: The current method is already extensive, and many observed failures have an existing rule aimed precisely at them. Adding one more rule for each review finding would make compliance more costly without resolving the decision that failed. This round's useful distinction is between a missing rule, a defective example, a conflicting instruction, an unexecuted check and a judgment that proved wrong.

instances.detail: Over-allocation of routine constant arithmetic survives despite existing audience and proof-allocation rules.
The rule already asks an example to block a likely false inference; the current examples only partly test the distinction the novelty discussion needs.
The positive-rewrite specimen needs qualification after the formal-route correction.

entry.existing_safeguard: The stage account says the local rules were generalized, merged and split by purpose rather than accumulated verbatim.
entry.what_to_do_instead: For each accepted method finding, identify its failure class and edit the smallest existing rule or specimen that owns it. Prefer one decisive acceptance task over another paragraph of exhortation. Keep general principles general; preserve this construction's examples as examples. Retire redundant or contradictory wording when a rule is strengthened.
entry.acceptance_check: The revised method is easier to apply, and a reviewer can explain which existing decision would change on the next paper in another field.

locator.quote: we charge only for the bits it reads.

entry.feedback: I know circuit depth, gate count and qubits as resources. This sentence does not quite tell me that a large input-independent circuit, arbitrary workspace and preparation of the input oracle are all outside the resource being optimized. Later the enormous certificate array and the free Walsh transform make that omission consequential.
entry.why_it_matters: I can read the fourth power as a physical running-time improvement and then find the construction implausible for the wrong reason.
entry.advice: Give one brief resource convention here, naming oracle calls as the cost and gate/workspace costs as uncounted. Watrous’s query-model lesson makes this distinction before algorithm analysis; the record already supplies the exact convention in §2.3.

locator.quote: A quantum algorithm reads through the oracle $O_x|j,b,w\rangle=|j,b\oplus x_j,w\rangle$

entry.feedback: This is my first actual stopping point. I can manipulate matrices, but no convention identifies the ket as a basis vector, the three registers as factors, or XOR as the reversible way to copy a queried bit. Naming positions, answer bits and workspace in the next clause does not supply those operations.
entry.why_it_matters: The sentence that should establish the simplest shared vocabulary instead makes the quantum half inaccessible before the problem is motivated.
entry.advice: Explain the action on an ordinary basis input with answer bit zero first, then explain linear extension and why one oracle call counts once. The supplied survey introduces the vector and measurement conventions before writing this oracle.

locator.quote: we charge only for the bits it reads

entry.feedback: There is no familiar function on which I can calibrate a query count before seeing the extremal result. A four-bit OR would let me distinguish the fixed input, the answer, the algorithm’s adaptive observations, and the cost. At present all four arrive inside an unfamiliar construction.
entry.why_it_matters: I cannot judge what is remarkable about an exponent four without first seeing an ordinary quadratic benchmark and what a lower bound means.
entry.advice: Use one small OR decision-tree example and state its large-input randomized versus quantum scaling before the new family. Keep it short enough that the construction remains the main subject.

locator.quote: with error at most $1/3$ on every input

entry.feedback: The definition is correct, but I have not yet separated probability over the algorithm’s randomness from probability over an input distribution. A reader coming from average-case algorithms can read this as success on two thirds of inputs. That misunderstanding becomes costly when μ is introduced in Section 5.
entry.why_it_matters: I will misread the hard distribution as part of the definition of R, rather than as a proof device for a worst-case measure.
entry.advice: Give one sentence or tiny contrast using a fixed input and many coin outcomes; explicitly locate the probability. Later, recall this when the hard input distribution is introduced.

locator.quote: For a **total** function, defined on every input

entry.feedback: I can parse the definition of a total function, but I do not yet understand why totality is the decisive mathematical restriction. The next display asks me to understand an optimal exponent over all total functions before I have seen one easy promise problem become difficult on extending its domain.
entry.why_it_matters: The central result appears to be about a technical choice of domain rather than a restriction on the source of quantum advantage.
entry.advice: Use a brief already available example or accepted fact to explain what excluding inputs can buy. The one-sided one-bit promise in record §2.6 is an economical illustration of why completing a promise changes a problem; distinguish that illustration from a speedup example.

locator.quote: $k$-fold Forrelation (Sections 1 and 3)

entry.feedback: The first example used to explain the model is the unfamiliar problem that the rest of the article has to teach. My circuit-course knowledge gives me Grover search, but it is not used as a baseline until the historical discussion.
entry.why_it_matters: I cannot tell which part of the coming fourth-power separation exceeds the familiar square-root search advantage.
entry.advice: Before the Forrelation sentence, use the already cited OR/Grover baseline to fix what a quadratic relation between R and Q means. One example is enough; do not add another preliminary survey.

locator.quote: For a **total** function, defined on every input,

entry.feedback: The definition is correct, but my first-course intuition treats a promise as information guaranteed by an experiment. I need to see that totality asks for a correct Boolean answer on every bit string, not that the oracle becomes less quantum or its input is measured.
entry.why_it_matters: Without that distinction, the reason this theorem is compatible with large promise-problem separations remains obscure.
entry.advice: Use a very small contrast, such as unique search versus OR with no promise on the number of marked positions. Keep the manuscript’s stronger all-input query-cap convention explicit.

locator.quote: quantum cost $O_k(1)$ and classical cost about $m^{1-1/k}$

entry.feedback: The first asymptotic statement has a subscripted big-O before the role of k is explained. I know ordinary big-O, but I need to know that the hidden constant can depend on k, that m is growing, and that the cost is queries rather than gates.
entry.why_it_matters: Without that convention the later warning about fixing k looks like a technical caveat rather than part of the meaning of the first claim.
entry.advice: Explain O_k at its first use, with m as the growing parameter. Retain the later quantifier example for the stronger point about nonuniform thresholds.

locator.section: Introduction, definition of the optimal exponent
locator.quote: For a **total** function, defined on every input, $R$ is bounded by a polynomial in $Q$

entry.feedback: The prose moves from totality straight to an infimum over a family of inequalities. I can read the set notation, but the question it answers needs one ordinary sentence: one constant and one power must work for every total function of every input length. The additive one is also unexplained here, although the companion explains it.
entry.why_it_matters: I may think the theorem is a relation for this one constructed family, or that its exponent is a limit of R/Q, instead of an optimal universal power.
entry.advice: State the universal-versus-existential task before the infimum, and explain the harmless shift by one in a short parenthesis. Reuse the companion’s existing conceptual explanation without adding a new technical discussion.

locator.quote: \alpha_{\rm tot}=\inf

entry.feedback: An infimum over exponents, a universal constant, and a universal class of functions arrive before I have a concrete value of R or Q. An analyst understands the quantifiers, but must carry two ungrounded complexity measures through them.
entry.why_it_matters: The first serious expenditure of attention is on formal packaging of the conclusion rather than on the phenomenon.
entry.advice: Explain the universal comparison in words and establish a concrete benchmark first. Keep the exact definition accessible, but let its full quantifier analysis earn its place in §6.

entry.feedback: The first theorem gives the coefficient 1/400 and a sixth power of a logarithm before I know what a column or a certificate is. These are valid quantitative details, but their visual weight makes them look like the discovery I should remember.
entry.why_it_matters: The first-page memory load is spent on constants that are deliberately loose, while the two mechanisms generating the exponent remain abstract.
entry.advice: Lead the explanatory theorem statement with the two exponents and put the explicit numerical version immediately after the mechanism, or visually subordinate the constants. Keep exact bounds available; change their teaching priority.

locator.quote: a certificate that $F=1$ sits in one of them.

entry.feedback: Here I understand certificate to mean a collection of observed input values that forces F=1. Later the selected cell contains transcripts and pointers, but verifying the witness also reads the winning string and bits in other columns. The object stored in a cell and a certificate in the decision-tree sense are not obviously the same object.
entry.why_it_matters: I initially picture a self-contained proof inside one cell and then cannot see why verification needs a search over tests outside it.
entry.advice: Distinguish the stored witness data from the input bits its verification consults at this first use. The later local-test list already provides the needed content; this needs a conceptual label, not a new definition-heavy subsection.

locator.quote: a certificate that $F=1$ sits in one of them

entry.feedback: Certificate is the first unfamiliar conceptual noun in the main explanation. I know NP certificates, but here the certificate itself consists of ordinary input bits, and a cell’s contents need checking. I have not yet been told whether this is an external witness, advice to the algorithm, or a designated part of the input.
entry.why_it_matters: I can build an entirely wrong picture of who supplies the certificate and what the algorithm initially knows.
entry.advice: Introduce a certificate here as proposed evidence stored in the input whose consistency must be checked. Save the formal winning conditions for Section 2.

locator.quote: The input of $F_{k,m}$ has $m$ columns

entry.feedback: The opening began with n input bits, but the theorem is now parametrized by m. I can easily assume m is another name for input length, even though one column already contains an m-bit string and a large cell array.
entry.why_it_matters: I may report the theorem as R about n squared and Q about square-root n, which is not what is proved.
entry.advice: At the first column sentence say that m is the number of columns, not the total number of input bits; point to Section 3 for the size. A compact parameter key would prevent repeated backtracking.

locator.quote: R\approx m^{2-1/k}=(\sqrt m)^{4-2/k}\approx Q^{4-2/k}

entry.feedback: The approximation chain is memorable but it treats an upper bound on Q and a lower bound on R as though both were established equalities. I need to know what I am allowed to infer from these one-sided estimates.
entry.why_it_matters: I may think the construction proves a matching asymptotic formula for each query complexity, rather than the separation the argument actually requires.
entry.advice: Label this as exponent bookkeeping and briefly say that only Q’s upper bound and R’s lower bound are needed. In Section 6 return explicitly to that distinction when forming the ratio.

locator.quote: Learning them costs about $L$ queries to the column, the classical cost of one instance

entry.feedback: This still sounds as if learning all r answers is possible in about the cost of one answer. Section 5 proves that spending at most L in total makes a correct address very unlikely; it does not establish an O(L) algorithm for learning the whole address. I see the lower-bound intention, but the verb and cost phrase suggest an achievable cost.
entry.why_it_matters: I may try to reconcile the r independent instances by inventing a nonexistent classical shortcut, or by thinking the r factor was accidentally forgotten.
entry.advice: Express this as a lower-cost obstruction: below L total queries the whole address is unlikely to be right. Keep the conclusion that a constant fraction of columns must be paid for, without suggesting an upper bound for learning all answers.

locator.quote: Tal reached $8/3-o(1)$

entry.feedback: The history asks me to remember several author groups, three exponents, pointers, cheat sheets, AND-OR and optimal partial separation before I have seen any concrete input. It is useful credit, but at this stage I cannot attach most of the names to an idea.
entry.why_it_matters: The examples-first promise is delayed by a literature tour whose distinctions I cannot yet retain.
entry.advice: Keep the essential predecessor and the old cubic obstruction near the opening, but move the detailed chronological sequence to the point where its ingredients have names and examples. Preserve all credit.

locator.quote: Let us see why that route stops at three.

entry.feedback: This is an interesting comparison, but it introduces AND–OR, composition, certificate size and three different cost expressions before I have seen the present function. I can check the powers algebraically without understanding why those are the quantities being multiplied.
entry.why_it_matters: The historical explanation temporarily becomes a second construction to learn on the first page.
entry.advice: Keep the fact that the earlier recipe reaches the cube in the opening. Put its detailed arithmetic after the current board or after the two current costs have been explained, with a direct comparison of the old and new bottlenecks.

locator.quote: every input has a certificate of $n$ bits.

entry.feedback: I can compute an AND of ORs but do not yet know certificate complexity. The text uses the small certificate as the decisive feature of the older construction without showing what is actually recorded.
entry.why_it_matters: The reason for composing with AND–OR still looks like an arbitrary algebraic trick.
entry.advice: Describe the two certificate shapes in words: one witnessed 1 in every row for a 1-output, or one completely zero row for a 0-output. This uses the same n-by-n object already named; no new construction is needed.

locator.quote: every input has a certificate of $n$ bits

entry.feedback: This is the pivotal reason for inserting AND-OR, but no two-by-two example shows the certificate. For a one-input the witness picks a one in every row; for a zero-input it gives a whole zero row. Without those two cases the claim looks like another complexity fact I must import.
entry.why_it_matters: I do not learn why making a partial function total used to cost the extra quantum factor, which is one of the stated teaching goals.
entry.advice: Show the two certificate shapes on a two-by-two AND-OR input before using the general n-bit certificate claim. This is an explanation of the existing construction, not an additional theorem.
entry.outside_source: Packet: Aaronson–Ben-David–Kothari, Separations in query complexity using cheat sheets, §3.1.

locator.quote: This account is written for a graduate student who knows the query models above

entry.feedback: This sentence does not describe my assigned background: I am a research mathematician without query complexity or quantum computing. The following list assumes Grover search, amplitude amplification, uncomputation and Yao. Naming these prerequisites is an improvement over hiding them, but it has not made the account suitable for this panel.
entry.why_it_matters: The text resolves a teaching problem by declaring a different reader, so the advertised newcomer endpoint remains unmet.
entry.advice: For the requested audience, supply small bridges or state precisely accepted inputs before their use. Preserve the useful prerequisite links; do not count the stronger prerequisite list as a completed repair. This is the remaining consequence of round-six finding SX-001, not a claim that the list is absent.

locator.quote: This account is written for a graduate student who knows the query models above

entry.feedback: This quietly changes the entry requirement. I know quantum circuits, but a line defining R and Q does not teach minimax, decision trees or complexity notation, and the later sentence simply assumes Yao’s principle. The packet’s physicist/engineer reader cannot satisfy the advertised contract by reading the opening paragraph.
entry.why_it_matters: The exposition can be useful to me, but its present prerequisite statement makes failures of explanation look like failures of preparation.
entry.advice: State an attainable entry route for a circuit-trained newcomer. Explain the small amount of decision-tree/minimax language used at its point of use, and keep the longer proof as an optional destination. Do not merely expand the prerequisite list.

locator.quote: This account is written for a graduate student who knows the query models above

entry.feedback: The audience has shifted away from me. Naming Grover search, amplitude amplification, uncomputation and Yao accurately describes what the current text assumes, but I have probability, linear algebra and algorithms, not those subjects. The round-six repair made the prerequisites explicit without supplying the bridge required by this round’s newcomer brief.
entry.why_it_matters: I can no longer treat the document as a route into query complexity; it reads as a revision sheet for a course I have already taken.
entry.advice: Keep the honest prerequisite description, but add a short entry route that teaches the few operations actually used. State which parts of the quantum proof may be accepted as a named contract on that route; do not solve the mismatch merely by raising the declared audience.
entry.outside_source: Packet: Buhrman–de Wolf, Complexity Measures and Decision Tree Complexity, §3.3; de Wolf, Quantum Computing: Lecture Notes, §§2.4, 7.1–7.3.

locator.quote: By the end, the reader should be able to build the function on a four-column board

entry.feedback: The explicit outcomes give me things to test rather than a vague promise of understanding. The separate quantum and lower-bound routes are also useful: I can decide which argument to study carefully and which bound to accept provisionally.
entry.why_it_matters: These are concrete navigational aids for a student who cannot absorb both proof technologies at once.
entry.advice: Keep the outcomes and the two routes. Make the later questions test each promised outcome, including the address-prediction reduction.

locator.quote: Let us read $\Phi$ geometrically.

entry.feedback: This is the first point at which the construction becomes familiar mathematics: a normalized inner product, an orthogonal transform, an aligned vector and an orthogonal one. I can check the values without knowing a quantum algorithm.
entry.why_it_matters: It gives the mathematician a stable interpretation to carry into the later projection experiment.
entry.advice: Keep the geometric paragraph and its three comparisons. Use this interpretation again when the general k-fold expression appears, rather than treating it as a disposable small-case calculation.

locator.quote: The first block of $a^+$ matches it exactly

entry.feedback: The parallel, antiparallel and orthogonal vectors are the first point where I can independently explain the function to someone else. They connect the sign convention, the Walsh transform and the promise using linear algebra I already know.
entry.why_it_matters: This is an effective bridge from an unfamiliar computational problem to familiar mathematics.
entry.advice: Retain all three cases and the geometric interpretation. Do not compress them into a table of function values without the vector relation.

locator.quote: this **projection experiment** succeeds with probability $\Phi^2$.

entry.feedback: The matrix calculation is transparent, but the physical meaning of projection is not yet established for my reader. Does projecting mean applying a linear map and renormalizing, or making a random measurement with two outcomes? The probability statement uses a rule that has not been introduced.
entry.why_it_matters: I can reproduce the scalar Phi but cannot explain why the same scalar yields a bounded-error query algorithm.
entry.advice: Give the two-outcome measurement rule at this first use: the squared norm of the projected component is its probability, and the complementary component is the other outcome. A short bridge from finite-dimensional linear algebra is enough; no full quantum course is needed.

locator.quote: Start in $u$, apply the signs $z_2$ with one query

entry.feedback: The vector calculation is readable, but this is where a circuit-trained reader would profit from a tiny circuit tying the two four-component sign vectors to a two-qubit index register. The prose never puts the classical input bits, phase oracle calls and ordinary Hadamards on one picture.
entry.why_it_matters: I can check the scalar product without being able to identify which operations are charged as queries.
entry.advice: Use a small circuit or operation strip for this existing example, with the two input-dependent diagonal operations marked as the charged calls. The circuit presentation in the supplied Forrelation paper and Bansal–Sinha slides is a useful model.

locator.quote: Since $\Phi=u^{\mathsf T}D_{z_1}HD_{z_2}u$

entry.feedback: D_z appears in the small experiment before it is defined as the diagonal matrix of signs in §3. A physicist will probably infer the meaning, but that inference is being required exactly when the example is supposed to remove notation barriers.
entry.why_it_matters: A reader checking the matrix dimensions must stop and guess a definition.
entry.advice: Define D_z on first use in §1; §3 can recall the notation rather than introducing it again.

locator.quote: and project onto $u$.

entry.feedback: I recognize projective measurement, but the experiment’s actual measurement instruction is missing. Testing overlap with u is not a computational-basis measurement until the fixed change of basis is supplied.
entry.why_it_matters: The step that turns the displayed amplitude into an executable experiment remains implicit.
entry.advice: Say that the final fixed Hadamard transform followed by the all-zero outcome test measures this projection. Record §3.3 already gives this implementation; a short reminder suffices.

locator.section: 1. Three eight-bit inputs, interpretation of the three trials
locator.quote: so a single run happens to decide them

entry.feedback: The sentence follows probabilities for all three inputs, but a− is outside the domain and has no required Boolean answer. In ordinary reading, deciding all three sounds like a− has been classified correctly as a one-input. The next paragraph explains the distinction, but this sentence first creates the wrong impression.
entry.why_it_matters: The central distinction between acceptance by a decoder and membership in the promise becomes blurred at exactly the example designed to teach it.
entry.advice: Limit the decision claim to the two promised inputs and describe the off-promise acceptance separately. No mathematical change is needed.

locator.quote: the one-input $1111\,1000$ has $\Phi=1/2$

entry.feedback: This useful fourth input fixes the misleading perfection of the first three trials, but the answer is handed to me immediately. It is the easiest place to check whether I can translate bits to signs and then square an amplitude.
entry.why_it_matters: The section demonstrates the conventions without testing whether I can now use them; its later census is less valuable than this immediate practice.
entry.advice: Let the reader compute Φ and the acceptance probability for this already present input before revealing them. This can be a one-line check, not another full worked example.

locator.quote: The experiment accepts $a^-$ with certainty, just as it accepts $a^+$.

entry.feedback: This is an effective use of a quantum phenomenon that I already understand: an acceptance probability loses the sign of an amplitude. It turns an abstract promise restriction into a concrete obligation of the total construction.
entry.why_it_matters: It gives the later domain bit a specific job rather than introducing it as defensive bookkeeping.
entry.advice: Keep the negative example and its immediate return in the changed-board test. The short argument is more useful than another numerical threshold estimate.

locator.quote: At this size the classical bound is empty

entry.feedback: The explicit statement that the tiny instance illustrates conventions rather than asymptotic hardness is essential. It prevents the hand computation from being presented as empirical evidence for the separation.
entry.why_it_matters: Without it I might try to infer a classical lower bound from an eight-bit example that is easy to enumerate.
entry.advice: Preserve this limitation, and make every later reuse of the tiny board inherit the same scope.

locator.quote: Of all $256$ inputs, $104$ are one-inputs

entry.feedback: The exact census does not advance the argument I have just learned. The symmetry of positive and negative cases is illuminating; the number 104 is not subsequently used.
entry.why_it_matters: I spend attention deciding whether the frequency of promised inputs matters for the hard distribution, even though μ is not the uniform distribution on these 256 strings.
entry.advice: Keep the sign-negation symmetry in the main explanation and mark the exact census as an optional convention check or leave it in the record. Explicitly separate it from the later hard law.

locator.quote: $L_{2,4}=\lfloor 2/4\rfloor=0$

entry.feedback: The warning that this tiny example proves no lower bound is useful, but the symbol L has not yet been defined beyond the opening approximation. I must infer the exact denominator from a formula that will appear in Section 3.
entry.why_it_matters: A welcome scope clarification ends the first example with a forward-reference calculation I cannot independently reconstruct yet.
entry.advice: Say that the exact lower-bound budget will be defined in Section 3 and is zero here, or give the short defining substitution with the warning. Keep the scope warning itself.

locator.quote: We describe one column in general, then a four-column board.
