entry.feedback: The list is correct, but the surprising member is J_i itself: the simulator is allowed to know the target column’s zero even though the original algorithm is trying to discover hidden structure. This does not help it compute s_i because J_i is independent of the target A tuple.
entry.why_it_matters: A specialist checking the reduction may pause over whether free information has accidentally solved part of the target task.
entry.advice: Add the reason this apparently generous information is harmless: the predictor’s target is the vector of P-values, not the erased zero. Keep the target strings, address and transcripts excluded.

locator.quote: without a query to the cell's contents.

entry.feedback: This is the decisive reduction step. The coordinate of a prospective cell query already encodes the whole address, so the simulator stops before observing any planted content.
entry.why_it_matters: It turns a search event into a vector-answer predictor without assuming the algorithm explicitly computes that vector.
entry.advice: Keep this sentence and the time-four row of the toy simulator; give them visual priority over routine constant arithmetic.

locator.quote: The distinction in (21) between the joint event and success conditional on nonheaviness

entry.feedback: This is the second explicit counterexample to conditioning on a cap event in the same chapter. The first uses two AND instances and a redundant query; this one uses one promised AND instance and mirrors the simulator more directly. Their different teaching jobs are not announced.
entry.why_it_matters: A continuous reader can feel that the same warning is being proved twice without knowing which example to retain mentally.
entry.advice: State the distinction in purpose: the first exhibits loss of a product law under a union of transcript rectangles; this one isolates the actual nonheavy event. Link them rather than treating the second as a fresh surprise.

locator.quote: The factor \(m\) cancels,

entry.feedback: The average over the independent selected column, rather than a union over all columns, is exactly where an unnecessary factor m is avoided. This is correctly made explicit.
entry.why_it_matters: The exponent bookkeeping depends on preserving this averaging step.
entry.advice: Keep the explanation, including the distinction between the time union and the column average.

locator.quote: In the Lean development an older core theorem proves

entry.feedback: The main discrepancy calculation is interrupted by the history of core and Paper wrappers. G.8 already explains signed versus absolute endpoints and their proof routes.
entry.why_it_matters: The reader is trying to check a three-term bound, but is sent into declaration genealogy before the numerical contradiction.
entry.advice: Keep the absolute-value inequality in the body and move or reduce this implementation-history paragraph to its G.8 destination.
entry.prior_round_status: Residual evidence prose after the round-six move to Appendix G; the move itself is acknowledged as successful.

locator.quote: the paper's exact logarithmic tail:

entry.feedback: The asymptotic o(1) calculation comes before the simpler finite m^-10 estimate that actually proves the stated generic theorem for every allowed m. Both are correct, but their order briefly suggests an extra large-m hypothesis is being introduced.
entry.why_it_matters: The reader has to wait to learn that the construction reduction itself needs no new threshold once 1≤L≤m.
entry.advice: Lead with the finite estimate used for the contradiction and present the preprint’s exact tail as a comparison or recovery note. Preserve the numbered source claim.

locator.quote: This comparison identifies the literature input and the strength we use.

entry.feedback: The lower-bound chapter gives every ingredient but never collects the losses in one place: the planting reduction preserves mL; the address length is chosen to defeat the time union; the two floors lose only constants; the deliberately weaker Forrelation L supplies the displayed logarithmic denominator.
entry.why_it_matters: This is the exact accounting a separations reader wants when judging where exponent four is won or lost.
entry.advice: Add a compact loss ledger referring to the existing inequalities. Do not derive a stronger bound; simply classify each existing loss as constant, logarithmic or a power of m.

locator.quote: Both floors are bounded in the direction a lower bound needs.

entry.feedback: The record gives an actual range t≥8, checks positivity before applying the floor estimate, and uses the same circuit as the upper bound. This is more useful than a vague “absorb the floors into constants”.
entry.why_it_matters: It keeps the numerical endpoint and the same-family quantifiers auditable.
entry.advice: Preserve the proof, while keeping it visually subordinate to the simulator and budget accounting.

locator.quote: We now combine the two bounds for the same functions and compute the infimum.

entry.feedback: Section 1 already gives the full ratio inequality and its limiting argument. Section 7 then restates the definition, the theorem, the same-function requirement, the floor conversion and the ratio. The complete proof belongs here, but the opening currently duplicates much of it.
entry.why_it_matters: The reader encounters the easy endpoint at greater length than the difficult reduction that earns it.
entry.advice: Choose one location for the full parameter argument; let the other state the idea and point to it. Preserve the explicit order of quantifiers in at least one visible display.

locator.quote: At \(\alpha=4-2/k\) the power gap

entry.feedback: The strictness is correctly explained. For fixed k the ratio method excludes powers below 4−2/k; the endpoint does not follow because of the logarithmic denominator.
entry.why_it_matters: This is the precision the exposition needs when describing k=2 and the cubic threshold.
entry.advice: Keep this sentence as the canonical wording for the derived accounts.

locator.quote: We now choose $k=\lfloor\sqrt{t/20}\rfloor$

entry.feedback: The schedule appears as a choice before the reader sees why that scale is natural. The later expression 40k+ℓ/k contains the competing losses: increasing k reduces the 1/k classical loss but increases the exponential-in-k quantum prefactor.
entry.why_it_matters: The long numerical derivation can look like an arbitrary successful substitution instead of a readable balance of the existing estimates.
entry.advice: Motivate the schedule using those two terms before substituting it. Keep the current proved schedule and constants; no optimization or stronger theorem is requested.

locator.quote: The chain gives the constant $474$; we state $508$,

entry.feedback: This explains an editorial synchronization choice with the companion, rather than a mathematical necessity. The record is supposed to be the source from which the shorter account is derived; citing the shorter account as the reason for the constant reverses that direction.
entry.why_it_matters: The reader sees revision history inside an otherwise self-contained inequality chain.
entry.advice: Describe 508 simply as a convenient conservative bound in the mathematical text, and record the cross-document synchronization outside it. Keep the agreed value if that is the chosen presentation.

locator.section: §7.3: initial range of the growing-k estimate
locator.quote: when $\varepsilon(\ell)\ge4$ the inequality below holds trivially.

entry.feedback: This is correct, and it reveals that t≥80 is a validity threshold, not the point at which the displayed exponent gives a useful positive separation. The distinction is easy to miss because the final theorem-like display emphasizes “for every t≥80”.
entry.why_it_matters: An explicit constant-heavy estimate can appear quantitatively stronger than its first admissible values warrant.
entry.advice: Say that the interest of this schedule is the asymptotic approach of the exponent to four. Do not add another numerical threshold unless it serves a reader need.

locator.quote: although the argument gives no bound $R=\Omega(Q^4)$ for this family.

entry.feedback: The new uniform schedule is distinguished from an exact fourth-power lower bound. That distinction must survive even though all three formulations have “quartic” in their informal description.
entry.why_it_matters: It prevents an asymptotic exponent statement from being promoted to a constant-factor relation.
entry.advice: Keep this limitation attached to the growing-k conclusion and mirror it in any summary.

locator.section: Appendix A.2: correction history inside the proof
locator.quote: A separate older annex transcription inserted an extra square root around the entire denominator.

entry.feedback: The local adversary-prefactor comparison earns its place because it checks a specific mathematical statement. The older annex transcription story is a separate maintenance event and interrupts that comparison.
entry.why_it_matters: A reader needs the correct coefficient, the counterexample’s scope and the cited edition, not the history of an unrelated transcription.
entry.advice: Move the transcription history to Appendix F and leave the mathematical discrepancy and its precise limits here.

locator.quote: A maximum-degree face and Huang's signed cube

entry.feedback: The proof uses an actual restriction on a maximum-degree support, preserves its coefficient, and identifies a parity-agreement set of more than half the face. The eigenspace intersection then gives the required sensitivity witness.
entry.why_it_matters: This is the conceptual center of the universal quartic bound; replacing it by a chain of named inequalities would remove the explanation.
entry.advice: Keep the face restriction and dimension argument together, with the surrounding constant discussion secondary.

locator.quote: at that original \(x\)

entry.feedback: The proof explicitly puts every sensitive block at the same original input, even though the algorithm proceeds through successive restrictions.
entry.why_it_matters: Block sensitivity is defined at one input; merely producing a block sensitive somewhere at each round would not prove the product bound.
entry.advice: Preserve this sentence and the disjoint-support argument when tightening the proof.

locator.quote: E[prod_j V_j(tau') | tau] <= prod_j V_j(tau).

entry.feedback: The catalogue’s machine-style expressions are harder to read than the mathematical displays they index. This particular entry compresses a product, a conditional expectation and a transcript update into plain text.
entry.why_it_matters: The reference destination makes the reader reconstruct notation at precisely the moment they want a quick statement check.
entry.advice: Offer readable mathematical rendering next to the stable claim identifier, while retaining the exact ledger payload in its machine-readable file. Do not silently change a hashed statement.

locator.quote: Sections 6.2–6.7 prove the planted lower bound.

entry.feedback: There is no §6.7 in the current record. The former formal-scope section was moved to G.8; the proof now ends in §6.6.
entry.why_it_matters: A catalogue that is meant to be the stable navigation destination should not refer to a vanished section.
entry.advice: Change the range to the current proof sections and link formal scope separately to G.8.
entry.prior_round_status: Stale catalogue prose after the evidence-appendix move.

locator.quote: Let P be a partial function on km bits

entry.feedback: The body’s generic theorem permits a partial function on any finite coordinate set; this catalogue row specializes to km bits without specifying k in its local assumptions. It is narrower and less self-contained than the statement it is indexing.
entry.why_it_matters: A reader looking up the generic reduction cannot tell whether the dependence on the Forrelation block size is essential.
entry.advice: Align the catalogue’s quantified input dimension with the existing body statement, or explicitly label this as a specialized historical corpus row. This is a presentation correction, not a request for another theorem.

locator.quote: no joint growing-$k$ schedule is inferred.

entry.feedback: As a statement about all of Section 7 this is stale: §7.3 now derives a growing-k schedule from uniform estimates. The fixed-k bounds alone still do not justify substitution, but the catalogue paragraph does not make that restricted scope explicit.
entry.why_it_matters: The catalogue contradicts the new result a reader may have arrived to locate.
entry.advice: Restrict the warning to the fixed-k argument of §§7.1–7.2, and point to the separate existing uniform-estimate derivation in §7.3.
entry.prior_round_status: Incomplete propagation of the accepted round-six growing-k addition.

locator.quote: Quantum decision trees and semidefinite programming

entry.feedback: The entry combines the 2003 CCC metadata and DOI with the title of the May 2002 manuscript. The institutional record for the 2003 proceedings article gives “Quantum query complexity and semi-definite programming”. The difference is an edition/title issue, not a mathematical correction.
entry.why_it_matters: This appendix promises exact inspected editions; mixing the manuscript title with proceedings metadata weakens that promise.
entry.advice: Use the proceedings title for the 2003 DOI, or identify the 2002 manuscript separately. The original full text was not a proof source for this review.

locator.quote: Fix integers $k=\ell+1\ge2$

entry.feedback: Throughout the main construction ℓ means log₂m=2t; here it is reset to k−1. The definition is explicit, so there is no logical problem, but it makes comparison with the current threshold and growing-k estimate needlessly hazardous.
entry.why_it_matters: A reader may carry the dominant notation into a historical appendix whose purpose is comparison.
entry.advice: Use a visibly local auxiliary letter or warn at the opening that this appendix’s ℓ is unrelated to the construction’s bit length.

locator.quote: it neither constructs an algorithm nor disproves Bansal and Sinha's theorem.

entry.feedback: The scope of the version-specific calculation is carefully bounded. A failed comparison of two upper-bound expressions is not a counterexample to the source theorem, and the record says so.
entry.why_it_matters: It lets a reader assess a local source criticism without implying a research-level refutation.
entry.advice: Preserve the version, displayed-step locator and explicit non-refutation boundary.

locator.quote: **Pei Wu**

entry.feedback: The boldface author name reads as a correction to a previous draft. Correct attribution matters, but the current mathematical reader has no reason to infer that there was a competing identity.
entry.why_it_matters: Editorial emphasis interrupts a source comparison and makes an ordinary author credit look adversarial.
entry.advice: Use normal author typography; keep the full correct name and the version-specific theorem locators.

locator.quote: The only external mathematical input to (F60), beyond the proof above, is (F56).

entry.feedback: This states precisely what is transferred: a decision-tree Fourier-growth theorem, not the random-orthogonal or rorrelation distribution theorem. It also leaves the absolute constant unspecified.
entry.why_it_matters: It avoids conflating a stronger analytic tool with an automatically stronger theorem for a different promise.
entry.advice: Keep the source/transfer boundary and the fact that the main explicit proof does not require this comparison route.

locator.quote:
no exact-declaration
Comparator pass is supplied for these helpers.

entry.feedback: Inside a history appendix this can be true of the frozen return, but the nearby “current integration” wording obscures the date and the set of helpers. G.8 now names a later realized-caps endpoint accepted by Comparator. The reader should not have to infer which sentence belongs to which snapshot.
entry.why_it_matters: The status trail risks appearing contradictory even when every historical observation is accurate.
entry.advice: Attach a date/snapshot to each historical status paragraph and name the helper set being described. Keep current status in G.4 and do not promote one declaration’s result to another.
entry.prior_round_status: The broad round-six tense repair was made in F.1; this local present-tense ambiguity remains in F.5.

locator.quote: contains the names listed above

entry.feedback: After moving the formal declaration discussion to Appendix G, “the names listed above” has no obvious local referent in the exponent-history subsection.
entry.why_it_matters: A reader cannot tell which declarations the historical audit sentence covers without searching several different sections.
entry.advice: Name the relevant list or link to its exact current location, keeping the historical scope of the receipt unchanged.

locator.quote: This missing formal bridge is not an extra assumption in the proof of Proposition 3.3

entry.feedback: The record correctly separates the stronger full-state specification from the measured-label statement used by the final upper bound. It also distinguishes a built wrapper from a wrapper reached by a particular proof root.
entry.why_it_matters: This prevents an optional formal strengthening from being mistaken for a mathematical gap in the separation theorem.
entry.advice: Keep the boundary concise and source-specific. Do not turn the review into a request to complete the stronger formal target.

locator.quote: the ordinary finite-behavior reduction above,

entry.feedback: The formal-statement route can enter directly at Appendix G, but the relevant reduction is far away in §6.1. “Above” does not identify it, and there are several finite-mixture discussions in the record.
entry.why_it_matters: A reader checking the arbitrary-randomness boundary must search rather than follow a bounded proof route.
entry.advice: Link this phrase specifically to CL-independent-information, and distinguish the per-input cap condition from the finite seed-space statement.

locator.quote: No promise-support or hardness premise is needed for this row.

entry.feedback: This is a helpful boundary around equation (19). Its identity and search estimate belong to the independent zero-location experiment; the promised hard law is needed later for predicting the selected cell.
entry.why_it_matters: It shows which pieces of the lower bound remain valid independently of the Forrelation supplier.
entry.advice: Keep this separation of assumptions, especially when displaying the whole lower-bound chain.

locator.section: Appendix G.9: the status of the growing-k derivation
locator.quote: the rest of §7.3 is ordinary mathematics.

entry.feedback: The current record states exactly which displayed uniform estimate has a compiled supplier and which subsequent optimization is an ordinary derivation.
entry.why_it_matters: This is a more useful scope statement than a blanket claim that every displayed refinement has the same formal status.
entry.advice: Carry this distinction into any future summary that advertises the explicit growing-k family.

entry.rule_or_skill: register/REGISTER_RULES.md RG-02; skills/long-to-short/SKILL.md, paragraph-by-paragraph revision rule
entry.rule_quote: There is always something to improve in a sentence; a paragraph left unchanged needs a stated reason.
entry.classification: Rule incentive requiring refinement; causation is not established
entry.problem: The mandatory-rewrite presumption makes an unchanged, accurate paragraph look like an exception. In these drafts several full proofs preserve the necessary quantifiers while shorter summary or cap statements weaken them. The review cannot prove that RG-02 caused those edits, but the rule encourages churn exactly where logical fidelity has already been achieved.
entry.why_it_matters: A cosmetic revision can turn a fixed-time joint event into an ever-hit or conditional claim, or a fixed upper cap into a fixed realized count.
entry.recommendation: Retain the sequential reread, but permit a positive decision to preserve a paragraph because its purpose, inference and wording already work. Require a specific reader benefit before rewriting it. Treat changes to events, quantifiers and cost conventions as mathematical changes under RG-02's own limit.
entry.general_test: Before accepting a summary edit, compare its event, time scope, conditioning and quantifier order with the proof it summarizes. No new theorem or formal check is required.

entry.rule_quote:
Identify the result obtained at that
   destination and where the reader returns.
entry.classification: Existing sound rule was incompletely applied
entry.problem: The skills already require a complete outward-and-return journey. Current prose still points to the wrong companion section even when the file link resolves. A single tested journey does not cover all routes affected by section renumbering.
entry.why_it_matters: A reader who has recovered the omitted inference is sent to the wrong argument on returning. Structural link validity is weaker than semantic route correctness.
entry.recommendation: When a section moves, inspect its incoming references and its outgoing return instructions as one changed unit. Compare the visible number and topic with the actual destination. Prefer stable named anchors accompanied by readable topic labels. Refine the existing rule instead of adding another general navigation checklist.
entry.general_test: For each moved destination, follow one affected incoming reference and every distinct return label. Stop when the omitted inference and correct continuation are recovered.

entry.rule_quote:
Distinguish a theorem used in
   the proof, historical credit, an adapted construction and an explanatory
   comparison.
entry.classification: Historical comparison needs the same quantifier care as a theorem citation
entry.problem: The bibliography identifies the right pointer-function paper, but the companion changes its highlighted-zero condition into a condition on every zero. The exposition also names a proposed direct-pointer representation without carrying the source's reason for rejecting that representation in its own model.
entry.why_it_matters: Correct author attribution does not make the described antecedent accurate. It can conceal precisely what the new construction changes.
entry.recommendation: For adapted gadgets, compare the quantified objects, accepted inputs and access costs against the source definition. Record whether the source implements the gadget, proposes it, or explains an obstruction. Keep the changed interface local to the comparison.
entry.general_test: Can a reader instantiate the cited construction from the summary without imposing an extra condition or granting a cheaper access operation?

entry.rule_quote: A list of three genuinely parallel named objects is fine; the rule targets cadence.
entry.classification: Detector false positives; preserve the stated exception
instances: Expert measurement specimens naming Aaronson, Ben-David and Kothari, and Göös, Pitassi and Watson
entry.problem: The measured triads include author lists and meaningful mathematical groupings. The prose rule's exception already protects them, but its instruction to break three items into two or four makes the mechanical repair unusually tempting.
entry.why_it_matters: Changing an author list or obscuring the three real budgets would worsen accuracy and comprehension merely to move a style statistic.
entry.recommendation: Tag named authors and defined mathematical objects as exempt before considering rhythmic edits. Use a specimen-level judgement and state whether a flagged list is functional. Do not prescribe a different number of items.
entry.general_test: Would splitting or regrouping the list preserve the mathematical roles and make a concrete sentence easier to understand? If not, leave it.

entry.rule_or_skill: register/REGISTER_RULES.md RG-20 and RG-21; register/measurement.txt, apparatus and status vocabulary
entry.rule_quote: A detector points at sentences to reread; it never passes or fails a paper.
entry.classification: Measurement cannot determine allocation or useful evidentiary scope
entry.problem: Both shorter drafts have apparatus_rate zero, yet their formal sections can still overload the intended reader or join an evidentiary claim with the wrong causal connective. Conversely, the long record's high rate is partly expected in the dedicated evidence appendix. The statistic alone does not detect either issue.
entry.why_it_matters: A low score can coexist with an unhelpful verification paragraph, while an appropriate appendix can look like the worst prose in the bundle.
entry.recommendation: Judge formal prose by its job and location: what claim is checked, what the reader should inspect, and where the detailed scope lives. Separate the required proof route from optional evidence apparatus when interpreting rates. Keep the current detector-only warning explicit.
entry.general_test: Ask a reader to identify one checked statement and one material limitation without reading every declaration link. Do not infer success from a word-rate target.

entry.rule_or_skill: register/REGISTER_RULES.md RG-06 versus RG-21; reader_principles.md principle 2
entry.rule_quote: a long record replaces a reading guide with this paragraph.
entry.problem: RG-06 categorically replaces the long reading guide with one organization paragraph, while RG-21 permits a short guide separating required and optional routes. This record needs the latter because construction, independent Forrelation proof and formal-statement review have genuinely different prerequisite sets.
entry.why_it_matters: Following the more restrictive sentence can undo a successful repair and again force every reader through the longest route.
entry.recommendation: Give the role-based exception precedence: use one concise mathematical roadmap, with a short branching guide only where readers have different legitimate stopping points. Delete categorical wording that conflicts with that purpose.
entry.general_test: Can each intended reader find the necessary argument and stop without traversing an unrelated proof or evidence route?

entry.rule_quote: Say in the caption or the text what each mark means
entry.classification: Visual interpretation also needs consistency with declared data
entry.problem: The expert figure labels m=4 but draws eight positions per X string. The exposition's corresponding four-position board is correct. The caption can explain the meaning of every mark and still describe the wrong finite instance.
entry.why_it_matters: A diagram used to teach a finite construction carries mathematical data, not merely decoration. Copying a finding across superficially similar figures would also be a review error.
entry.recommendation: For an exact example, compare visible counts, addresses and edges with the stated parameter values. If the drawing is schematic, explicitly mark which lengths are schematic. Inspect each document's actual rendered figure independently.
entry.general_test: Can every displayed coordinate or edge be assigned to the claimed finite object without changing a parameter?

entry.rule_quote:
A repaired proof paragraph alone does not close
   the change.
entry.classification: Existing propagation rule should include negative claims and exercises
entry.problem: The new growing-k derivation coexists with an old catalogue claim that no such schedule is inferred. Exercise answers also strengthen bounded-error or endpoint claims beyond the main proof. These are claim-bearing locations even though they are not theorem statements.
entry.why_it_matters: Readers frequently rely on summaries and answers as their final understanding; correctness confined to the full proof is insufficient.
entry.recommendation: When a claim changes, include its negative scope statements, catalogue entries, captions and exercise answers in the same reconciliation pass. Compare each against the exact conclusion being used, including infimum versus endpoint and deterministic failure versus bounded-error rejection.
entry.general_test: List the changed claim's user-facing occurrences and ask whether each says the same thing, a deliberately weaker thing, or a stronger thing requiring support.

rule_or_skill: skills/record-to-expository/SKILL.md: Preconditions and inputs; Model the reader and frame the result
entry.general_problem: A prerequisite declaration can be treated as a successful teaching repair even when it narrows an audience fixed by the request. The skill already forbids this; the missing piece is enforcing that distinction at acceptance.

instances.current_quote: This account is written for a graduate student who knows the query models above

entry.recommended_change: For the first consequential use of each operation, record whether the fixed reader already knows it, the exposition teaches it locally, or a precisely stated input is accepted. If a broad new course prerequisite is needed, record an unresolved scope mismatch instead of marking the teaching request complete.
entry.scope_guard: Do not require remedial examples for operations actually supplied by the agreed audience, and do not forbid authors from choosing an audience when the task leaves that choice open.

entry.general_problem: An exercise answer can be checked against the author’s displayed parameter recipe rather than against the exact mathematical objective in its question. Endpoint assertions and infimum assertions are then conflated.

instances.current_quote: as $k=2$ for the cube, $k=4$ gives exactly $3.5$ and does not suffice.

entry.recommended_change: When an exercise uses a boundary value, explicitly identify its target conclusion: membership, non-membership, an attained extremum, an infimum bound, or failure of a particular sufficient test. Validate the answer against that conclusion, including nearby interior values.
entry.scope_guard: This is a targeted check for conclusions with different endpoint logic, not a requirement to add endpoint exercises to every theorem.

entry.general_problem: Conveniently exact components in a toy example can cause the write-up to make an entire probabilistic pipeline exact. A separate loss of modality occurs when a fixed maximum budget is described as a fixed realised execution.

instances.current_quote: and rejects $2$ and $4$ by the zeros in their own strings.
Every number of trials, iterations, stages and comparisons is fixed in advance

entry.recommended_change: At the output of each composed stage, retain whether the claim is deterministic, conditional, high probability, or capped in the worst case. Verify toy answers against every remaining stage of the actual algorithm, not merely the stage made exact by the chosen data.
entry.scope_guard: Do not turn this into a separate probability table for every example; use it where composition changes the status of a claim.

entry.general_problem: An exposition can execute several peripheral examples while leaving its main reduction as a named or described operation. Its exercises can then confirm local fluency without assessing the promised central inference.

instances.current_quote: it stops before the $(L+1)$-st forwarded query.
**[Question 3](#question-3).** An independent $I$ is hit with probability

entry.recommended_change: Identify the last established fact and the next required conclusion at the main reduction. Execute one existing small case across that transition, including its exceptional branch, then make a changed-case task ask the reader to carry out the same inference. Assess the transition rather than the number of examples or questions.
entry.scope_guard: Do not require a new example if the original proof already supplies an executable case, and do not infer human comprehension from an agent’s successful reconstruction.

entry.general_problem: A repair requesting full adaptive conditioning can introduce future information by replacing a vague local history with the completed transcript. The amount of information and its time index must be checked together.

instances.current_quote: condition on the whole transcript of the dummy run.

entry.recommended_change: For a claim about the next action or its conditional probability, state which observations precede that action and which remain random. Check that the event being predicted is not already determined by the conditioning. Preserve all relevant past observations without conditioning on future ones.
entry.scope_guard: The general lesson is temporal conditioning in adaptive arguments; it does not require formal filtration notation in a newcomer exposition.

rule_or_skill: skills/record-to-expository/SKILL.md: Procedure 2 and 6; Checks and example
entry.general_problem: A warning that a small example cannot instantiate a useful quantitative theorem can overstate the reason, turning failure of a hypothesis or a vacuous bound into nonexistence of a mathematical object. The skill already distinguishes an inconclusive test from a false conclusion.

instances.current_quote: At $m=4$ there is no hard distribution

entry.recommended_change: When delimiting a toy example, name the exact missing hypothesis or degenerate parameter and the conclusion that therefore cannot be drawn. Check whether the object still exists at that parameter, even if the quantitative argument is uninformative.
entry.scope_guard: Do not demand that every tiny example satisfy every asymptotic hypothesis; an honest illustration of geometry or definitions is sufficient.

rule_or_skill: skills/record-to-expository/SKILL.md: Model the reader and frame the result; Procedure 3
entry.general_problem: An optional supplier proof can remain embedded in the main route after a disposition says it was moved. Its exact constants then dominate the construction-specific inference that consumes only a contract.

instances.location: Section 4, Amplification with a fixed cap
instances.current_quote: Either way a trial succeeds with probability at least $9/40$.

entry.recommended_change: At a subroutine’s point of use, identify the exact contract the next step consumes and test the route with the proof skipped. Keep any construction-specific reason the contract applies, and put routine numerical derivation at its existing proof destination. Check the current rendered passage, not only the disposition’s stated intention.
entry.scope_guard: Do not remove a standard proof merely because it is standard; retain it if the agreed reader needs it to understand the local inference.

rule_or_skill: register/measurement.txt: exposition paragraph-length and question-share diagnostics
entry.general_problem: A register detector measures surface distribution, not whether a paragraph teaches the hard inference or whether an exercise assesses it. The same long-paragraph flag touches both a dispensable amplification recipe and the indispensable three-budget explanation.
entry.recommended_change: Triage flagged paragraphs by their instructional role: definition, worked operation, supplier proof, or transition. Pair exercise counts with the inference each question tests. Use measurements to find passages for review; do not normalize away a useful explanation or count questions as evidence of learning.
entry.scope_guard: Retain the detector as a search aid. This recommendation does not prescribe a universal paragraph length or a minimum exercise count.

locator.quote: The optimal randomized–quantum query exponent is four

entry.feedback: The title leaves out totality, the restriction on which the claim depends. A reader encountering the title alone in an index cannot tell that the statement concerns total Boolean functions. For promise problems there is no corresponding universal quartic relation.
entry.why_it_matters: The most searchable sentence has a wider apparent scope than the theorem.
entry.advice: Include the total-function setting in the title or a mathematically informative subtitle while retaining the credit to the original result.

locator.quote: Together these give $R\approx Q^{4-2/k}$.

entry.feedback: The abstract introduces k only through exponents. It never says what k is, that it is a freely chosen fixed integer, or why increasing it approaches four. The final sentence therefore asks the reader to infer the mechanism of the headline limit from an undefined parameter.
entry.why_it_matters: The abstract should work independently, and this is the point at which its conclusion is meant to become convincing.
entry.advice: Identify k as the order of the Forrelation problem and a parameter that may be chosen arbitrarily large; keep the formula only if that identification fits naturally.

locator.quote: A classical algorithm cannot locate the winning column's certificate

entry.feedback: This sounds like a statement about every winning input and every successful execution. The proof establishes a distributional obstruction to distinguishing a coupled pair with constant advantage; a lucky query can hit the certificate immediately, and easy positive inputs are not excluded.
entry.why_it_matters: The summary currently turns a lower-bound mechanism into an unqualified per-execution necessity.
entry.advice: Tie the sentence to the hard input distribution or to constant-probability success. This only calibrates the existing argument; it does not require another disclaimer or theorem.

locator.quote: We give the complete argument with explicit constants

entry.feedback: The promise of a complete argument is stronger than the reading experience. The companion cites the Forrelation lower bound, the circuit, the local-test lemma, and the universal upper bound, while the explicit uniform estimate is also delegated to the record. The end of §1 does disclose this carefully, but the abstract has already set a different expectation.
entry.why_it_matters: A referee needs to know whether this is a self-contained proof, an account of the two central analyses, or a formalisation companion before deciding how to read it.
entry.advice: Describe the actual scope of the companion positively at the first promise of completeness. Preserve the precise cited inputs, but do not make the reader wait through the introduction to discover the scope.
entry.round6_context: Round-six C12-opening-value sought a clearer account of what the companion adds. The current issue is the surviving scope promise, not missing credit.

locator.quote: A query algorithm reads its input one bit at a time

entry.feedback: As the common introduction to both models, this sentence suggests a classical sequence of inspected bits. The quantum model introduced two sentences later makes one coherent oracle call on a superposition of indices. Charging one oracle call is not the same operation as reading one definite bit.
entry.why_it_matters: The first explanation creates a model that the displayed oracle immediately has to repair.
entry.advice: Explain that the resource is access to individual input coordinates, then distinguish classical bit reads from coherent quantum oracle calls. A short conceptual adjustment is sufficient.

locator.quote: For total functions we measure the best polynomial relation between the two measures by

entry.feedback: The full infimum with four quantifiers arrives before the reader has met the gap between the known cubic examples and the quartic universal upper bound. It is mathematically sound, but the notation occupies the place where the central question should become clear.
entry.why_it_matters: An expert can parse the formula, yet has not been given a reason to retain the symbol alpha_tot.
entry.advice: State the question and the two benchmark exponents first, then use (1) to make the already-motivated question precise. Keep the uniform constant, since that is the quantifier later contradicted.

locator.quote: there are constants $c_k,C_k>0$ and $b_k$

entry.feedback: The declaration does not say what kind of number b_k is or whether it is nonnegative. Later the paper chooses six, but the first theorem should not leave the type of an exponent to a later paragraph.
entry.why_it_matters: This is a small avoidable pause in the main statement.
entry.advice: Specify the intended range of b_k, or use the explicit exponent if that is the statement the companion actually wants to foreground.

locator.quote: First, the constants are explicit:

entry.feedback: The first account of the companion’s contribution leads with b_k, c_k, C_k and an enormous threshold, followed by same-circuit bookkeeping and two additional observations. The construction has not yet been explained. The paragraph is accurate but makes numerical bookkeeping appear to be the reason to read the paper.
entry.why_it_matters: The central attraction is the interaction between hidden certificates, cheap comparisons and a weighted tournament. Its explanation is delayed by a ledger of refinements.
entry.advice: Lead with the explanatory or proof contribution and leave the exact numerical constants with the bounds they instantiate. Preserve the same-function point once beside the theorem or construction.
entry.round6_context: Round-six QX-017 proposed putting the mechanism ahead of constants; the current first contribution still foregrounds them.

locator.quote: The functions and both analyses are due to OpenAI.

entry.feedback: The attribution is immediate and unambiguous. Together with the subtitle and the introduction, it prevents the companion’s author line from being read as a claim to the discovery.
entry.why_it_matters: Clear credit lets the paper be assessed for its actual explanatory and formal contribution.
entry.advice: Retain an early plain attribution through any compression. Reduce repetition elsewhere if needed, rather than weakening this statement.

locator.quote: A quantum algorithm computes $g\circ h$ and Grover-checks a certificate

entry.feedback: At this point g has only been introduced as a partial function. The displayed quantum cost omits Q(g), and the polylogarithmic-Q(g) assumption appears in the following sentence. The intended special case is recoverable, but the display is temporarily presented as a general composition estimate.
entry.why_it_matters: A reader checking the predecessor arithmetic has to backtrack and restrict the scope of a formula already read.
entry.advice: State the polylogarithmic quantum-cost assumption before the display, or show its dependence on Q(g) and then specialise. Also name the total cheat-sheet function whose R and Q appear in the display.

locator.quote: Exponent $a$ with $R=Q^{a}$ (total $f$)

entry.feedback: The column heading uses equality although the historical entries are existential separation lower bounds up to logarithms, and the final row is a universal upper bound. These are different quantifier directions. The prose around the table is more precise than its heading.
entry.why_it_matters: The table is the part a reader is most likely to reuse independently, so it should not silently turn one-sided bounds into equalities.
entry.advice: Label the separating families with the lower-bound relation and put the universal upper bound in a visibly distinct row or column. Keep the chronological information.
entry.outside_source: https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.01937v2 ; supplied text, summary-of-results table and its explanation

locator.quote: Since $R(g)\le n$ for every $g$, the AND–OR recipe stops at the cube

entry.feedback: This is the right kind of historical explanation: it derives the exponent barrier of the named recipe instead of presenting a list of record exponents. It also avoids claiming that all possible cheat-sheet constructions stop at three.
entry.why_it_matters: The reader can now see what a nearly quartic construction has to change.
entry.advice: Keep the cost arithmetic and the restriction to the AND–OR recipe even if the surrounding history is shortened.
entry.round6_context: Round-six CX015 and QX-016 are visibly addressed; do not broaden this into an impossibility claim for cheat sheets.

locator.quote: The answers $s_i=(P(A_{i,1}),\dots,P(A_{i,r}))$ select one cell of the column.

entry.feedback: The overview assigns s_i to every column before saying what happens when one of its partial-function values is undefined. Section 2 resolves this correctly, and §1.2 later stresses arbitrary unpromised opponents, but the first construction description momentarily reads as a promised-input construction.
entry.why_it_matters: Totality is the central difficulty of this result, so this is not a harmless place to imply that all addresses exist.
entry.advice: Qualify the mathematical address by the promise at first use and distinguish it from the arbitrary decoded label. Keep the formal definition in §2 unchanged.

locator.quote: All of these are independent input bits.

entry.feedback: For the definition of a total function, these are freely specified coordinates, not random variables endowed with a product law. Figure 1 repeats the ambiguity by calling the A-blocks independent instances. Actual probabilistic independence is introduced only for the lower-bound distribution.
entry.why_it_matters: The same word carries a structural and then a probabilistic meaning at a point where joint independence will later be essential.
entry.advice: Use language of separate input coordinates or disjoint blocks in the construction and reserve probabilistic independence for §4. Check the Figure 1 label as part of the same edit.

locator.quote: $L\approx R(P)\approx m^{1-1/k}$

entry.feedback: The approximate-equality notation suppresses both logarithms and the distinction between a selected lower-bound threshold L and the actual optimal complexity R(P). Only L<R(P) is subsequently used. This shorthand also spreads to R and Q in the surrounding overview.
entry.why_it_matters: The mechanism is simple, but the notation encourages a stronger interpretation than the hypotheses establish here.
entry.advice: Say once that the overview suppresses logarithmic factors, and phrase L as the available hardness scale. Keep the exponent calculation; do not ask it to assert tightness of every intermediate measure.

locator.quote: The two inputs differ only in those two places.

entry.feedback: One of the two places is one bit and the other is an entire certificate cell. The phrase can be read as Hamming distance two, especially before the cell contents have been defined.
entry.why_it_matters: The lower bound uses a first-query-to-a-block event, not a coupling that changes just two bits.
entry.advice: Name the erased bit and the certificate block explicitly. The later hybrid inequality already uses the right events.

locator.quote: The winner's guarantee does not depend on the rival's address inputs

entry.feedback: This sentence isolates the unusual input guarantee that makes the construction total. The subsequent permission for arbitrary loser-versus-loser probabilities identifies the precise reason a standard ordering argument is inadequate.
entry.why_it_matters: It gives the reader a concrete invariant to look for in the tournament proof.
entry.advice: Retain it and the cost contrast with checking every candidate by a nested search. These are more valuable than another layer of constants.

locator.quote: without back pointers, the tree makes their functions hard even for bounded-error algorithms.

entry.feedback: The antecedent of their functions is broad, while this sentence has moved from the nearly quartic D-versus-Q function to a variant without back pointers. The contribution of the balanced tree and the identity of the variant become difficult to reconstruct.
entry.why_it_matters: The paragraph is supposed to explain why the older construction did not already settle the present question; vague reference undermines that comparison.
entry.advice: Name the back-pointer version and the no-back-pointer variant explicitly in the two relevant sentences, and keep the bound or model attached to its own variant.
entry.round6_context: Round-six CX002 repaired the missing comparison. This is a reference-resolution problem in the revised wording, not a request to restore the old omission.

locator.quote: Comparison search has close antecedents.

entry.feedback: This paragraph compares five nearby algorithmic settings before the present tournament has been stated. A specialist must hold total orders, fixed tournaments, sink-or-king search, approximate edge tests and arbitrary loser probabilities in working memory at once.
entry.why_it_matters: The useful comparison with the surviving-candidate construction is obscured by an introductory catalogue.
entry.advice: Keep the closest antecedent and the one mathematical distinction in the overview. Put the other comparisons beside Proposition 3 or in a compact related-work note, with their distinct guarantees preserved.

locator.quote: Section 2 defines the Forrelation promise and the total function.

entry.feedback: The roadmap is fused with a long list of omitted proofs, a second list of record-only arguments, a rule about what every other link means, and the exposition pointer. It arrives after almost four printed pages of introduction. This is too many reading decisions in one closing paragraph.
entry.why_it_matters: The reader has to classify the paper’s support architecture just when the construction should begin.
entry.advice: Use a short mathematical roadmap and place the indispensable scope statement next to the first promise of completeness. Let individual citations identify the optional longer arguments. Keep the exposition pointer as a simple destination.
entry.round6_context: Round-six SX-036 sought a shorter route paragraph. The current revision retains the right destinations but is still overloaded.

locator.quote: Fix $k\ge2$, $t\ge1$, $m=4^t$, $\ell=2t$ and $r=20\ell$

entry.feedback: This opening asks the reader to accept several apparently arbitrary choices simultaneously. The later integer-threshold calculation explains why a square power of two is convenient, and the union bound explains the constant twenty, but neither role is indicated here.
entry.why_it_matters: Even an expert benefits from knowing which choices are structural and which merely leave slack.
entry.advice: Give the role of the square power of two when it is introduced, and defer the numerical address-length constant until the lower-bound tail calculation or explain that its role is probability amplification.

locator.quote: The interference test of Aaronson and Ambainis

entry.feedback: Property (ii) contains its formal contract, a projection-based construction, coherent implementation, off-promise behaviour, a different interference test, and the reason either test suffices. All are useful, but the paragraph has no visual or grammatical division between the required property and optional implementation commentary.
entry.why_it_matters: The reader checking the theorem’s dependencies must extract the actual contract from its explanation.
entry.advice: Keep the quantified query/error statement together, then place the implementation and alternative-test explanation in a separate short paragraph. Preserve the promise/domain distinction that the revision correctly added.
entry.round6_context: Round-six QX-009 is addressed. The remaining issue is packaging, not absence of the sign-sensitive alternative.

locator.quote: one bit per non-input gate

entry.feedback: The exact formulas for the cell size and K later use rS, whereas the circuit is introduced only as having size S. Make explicit that S counts the non-input gate bits stored in a transcript, or that the transcript is padded to S bits if the convention differs.
entry.why_it_matters: The asymptotic estimate is unaffected, but exact equalities should not depend on an unstated circuit-size convention.
entry.advice: State the counting convention once beside the circuit and use it consistently in the two exact formulas.

locator.quote: since a winner's pointer into a second all-one column would find a zero there.

entry.feedback: The contradiction is grammatically compressed into a positive assertion that the pointer would find a zero in an all-one string. The reader has to supply “which is impossible” and infer which premise generated that assertion.
entry.why_it_matters: This is an easy argument that should feel immediate, rather than requiring a second reading.
entry.advice: Say directly that the second all-one column makes the first column’s required pointer condition impossible.

locator.quote: so in terms of its input length $Q(F_{k,m})\le n^{1/44+o(1)}$.

entry.feedback: The input-length exponent is introduced just before local verification and is never used in the rest of the proof. It opens a second quantitative axis at the moment the reader needs to understand certificates and tests. The displayed upper estimate on n alone also does not explain the direction of this conversion; the lower bound implicit in the exact formula is doing that work.
entry.why_it_matters: The paragraph distracts from the R-versus-Q mechanism and invites an unnecessary inverse-asymptotics check.
entry.advice: Move this optional size consequence to a remark or the record. If retained, point out the matching polynomial scale of n rather than presenting the conversion as following only from an upper bound.

locator.quote: when $i$ does not win some test fails at $(i,s)$ for every address $s$.

entry.feedback: The all-address statement is precisely the soundness property needed after an arbitrary decoder output, including an output from unpromised instances. It makes the later total-input verification argument short and convincing.
entry.why_it_matters: Weakening this to failure only at a true address would remove the key link between totality and verification.
entry.advice: Preserve the quantifier “for every address” and its connection to §3.3.

locator.quote: conditional on success its output state is $|g\rangle$ up to a global phase.

entry.feedback: The lemma advertises a returned-state conclusion stronger than the label distribution used in the main algorithm. The following sentence now tells us this explicitly, and §7 correctly distinguishes the formal procedures. The mathematical content is not wrong; it is simply more machinery than the main route needs to carry.
entry.why_it_matters: Readers spend attention on a state-level issue and later encounter a formal correspondence discussion about that unused strength.
entry.advice: Keep the cap and exact conditional label law on the main route. Put the retained-state strengthening with its proof or in the record if the companion does not otherwise use it.
entry.round6_context: The measured/retained-state distinction has been repaired. This finding is about weighting and does not allege that Lean identifies the two procedures.

locator.quote: Either way a trial succeeds with probability at least $9/40$

entry.feedback: The proof sketch spends substantial space on the rotation formula, the fifty-fifty trial mixture, the numerical threshold M and the constants 9/20 and 9/40. This is a standard ingredient whose role here is a fixed worst-case cap and the conditional label law.
entry.why_it_matters: The quantum section begins with implementation bookkeeping before its novel weighted tournament.
entry.advice: Compress the standard numerical derivation to the reason that bounded trials give a constant-success attempt, with precise citations and the existing record link. Retain the distinction from an expected-time guarantee.
entry.round6_context: Round-six QX-019 proposed a two-sentence sketch. The current sketch remains substantially longer, so this is unfinished compression rather than a new mathematical objection.

locator.quote: If exactly one column disqualifies the other, it is the victor; otherwise the smaller index is.

entry.feedback: The sentence is clear locally, but the section then alternates between victor, defeats, wins a comparison, dominant candidate and winner. Winner already has an exact predicate defined in §2, and the Appendix A counterexample depends on keeping that predicate separate from comparison dominance.
entry.why_it_matters: Terminology drift makes the later verification warning harder to absorb than it needs to be.
entry.advice: Use one verb for a pairwise comparison, reserve winner for the total-function predicate, and name dominance once when it is first needed.

locator.quote: coherently controlled by two candidate indices, reversible with all its workspace retained

entry.feedback: The proposition’s first sentence puts the circuit interface, reversibility, workspace policy, worst-case cap and probability relation in one chain of modifiers before reaching the algorithmic conclusion. These are real hypotheses, but their grammar obscures their roles.
entry.why_it_matters: A reader cannot readily separate the probabilistic theorem from the access conditions needed to implement it quantumly.
entry.advice: Separate the comparison interface from the assumptions on its probabilities, then state the output contract. Keep all hypotheses; this is an organisational edit.

locator.quote: The total weight halves in expectation at every step

entry.feedback: Equation (8) gives an upper bound of one half, not equality. The colloquial “halves” is understandable, but it is slightly less precise than the proof and can suggest an exact expectation identity.
entry.why_it_matters: The invariant is the main mechanism, so its prose summary should match the displayed inequality.
entry.advice: Say that the expected total weight is at most half its previous value.

locator.quote: For at most $T$ steps, and only while $W>0$

entry.feedback: The process may stop before T steps, but the next paragraph speaks of the weight after T steps. The intended convention is to keep W=0 after stopping. It is easy to infer, yet this is exactly the sort of small convention a reader auditing the Markov argument must settle.
entry.why_it_matters: Without the absorbing convention, the random variable used at time T has not quite been defined on stopped histories.
entry.advice: State that after W reaches zero it remains zero for the remaining analysis steps. No algorithmic change is needed.

locator.quote: We replace membership in that set by the weight $w_i=\prod_b a_{i\rho_b}$

entry.feedback: This is the paper’s most informative comparison with a predecessor. It identifies the mathematical object that changes, rather than merely saying the tournament is more general.
entry.why_it_matters: It tells a specialist how to transfer existing intuition while also explaining why arbitrary comparison probabilities can be tolerated.
entry.advice: Keep this sentence and its derivation from fresh comparison workspaces. Do not bury it in the related-work catalogue.

locator.quote: The algorithm never computes the weights.

entry.feedback: This sentence anticipates the right objection. The following displayed state and the two masses w_i/m and W/m then explain how the intended distribution is obtained without explicitly evaluating the weights.
entry.why_it_matters: The reader can see an implementable quantum sampling mechanism rather than an idealised sampling oracle.
entry.advice: Retain the state display, fresh-workspace condition, conditional label law and measurement of the next pivot together.

locator.quote: conditional on the entire past.

entry.feedback: The proof does not assume that stage failures are independent or that globally conditioning on no failures leaves the ideal pivot law unchanged. Its history-by-history coupling is the correct explanation of the accumulated error.
entry.why_it_matters: This is a delicate point where a shorter but careless sentence would change the argument.
entry.advice: Preserve the stopped coupling and the observation that failure after the winner is listed cannot undo its inclusion.

locator.quote: We reject the candidate if a failing test is found and accept it otherwise

entry.feedback: The verification paragraph alternates between a failing local test, amplification reporting failure, rejection of a candidate and acceptance of an input. The logic is correct, but the word failure refers to both a detected defect and an unsuccessful search for a defect.
entry.why_it_matters: A reader can reverse the one-sided guarantee on a quick pass.
entry.advice: Name the search outcome as “a defect found” or “no defect found” and keep it distinct from the final accept/reject decision. Preserve the asymmetric soundness argument.

locator.quote: The error is therefore at most $T\varepsilon$ on zero-inputs

entry.feedback: The displayed comparison of zero- and one-input errors is compact enough that the different union bounds are easy to miss. There are T possible false acceptances on a zero-input; on a one-input it suffices that the listed winner’s one fresh decoding succeeds, which explains the single final epsilon.
entry.why_it_matters: The formula is correct, but a referee has to reconstruct why the verification contribution is not T epsilon in both cases.
entry.advice: Attach a short interpretation to each term, especially the single winner-decoding term in the one-input bound.

locator.quote: The exponent six in (2) comes from a deliberately loose count

entry.feedback: This paragraph expands a deliberately non-optimised bound through comparisons, padding, trials, iterations and verifications, then announces that nothing later depends on the logarithmic exponent. It is the densest routine accounting in the quantum proof.
entry.why_it_matters: The detailed arithmetic receives more emphasis than its role in the theorem warrants, and it interrupts the transition to the classical mechanism.
entry.advice: Keep the final upper bound and enough intermediate factors to justify its polynomial-logarithmic nature. Send the expansion and explicit constant to the already linked record.
entry.round6_context: Round-six QX-021 proposed compressing this count. The current paragraph still does nearly all of the bookkeeping in the main text.

locator.quote: by compactness the best worst-case success is attained and is below $2/3$.

entry.feedback: The opening paragraph contains the whole lower-bound roadmap, the general P,L hypotheses, a change of notation scope, compactness and minimax. The compactness sentence is defensible, but it is one more conceptual transition before the hard distribution is introduced.
entry.why_it_matters: The reader has to unpack the existence of mu while also remembering what the forthcoming coupling is supposed to accomplish.
entry.advice: Separate the choice of the hard law from the roadmap. Keep the strict-threshold reasoning together, with its fuller justification in the record if necessary.

locator.quote: We work with unnormalised measures, so that branches of probability zero need no conditioning.

entry.feedback: This gives a purpose to the proof’s formalism before introducing V_d. The short induction then tracks exactly the one factor changed by a query, which is a much better fit here than an opaque invocation of a general theorem.
entry.why_it_matters: It makes adaptivity and zero-mass branches comprehensible without burdening the companion with a long separate framework.
entry.advice: Preserve this sentence and the factorwise recurrence through compression.

locator.quote: Per-path allowances go back to Shaltiel's fair trees

entry.feedback: The literature paragraph shifts from hypotheses, to historical origin, to specific lemmas in Drucker, to a different theorem with a parameter substitution, then back to why this proof was selected. The content is useful but the sentence sequence makes the reader repeatedly change task.
entry.why_it_matters: The simple reason for the separate-cap lemma is less easy to find than the technical ancestry.
entry.advice: State the choice of lemma first, attach its provenance, and make the global-budget alternative a compact optional remark. Preserve the explicit fact that the global theorem also suffices.
entry.round6_context: Round-six CX001 is fixed. Do not reinstate the old suggestion that a global-budget theorem is unusable.

locator.quote: The two coupled inputs, here with $m=4$ and $I=3$.

entry.feedback: The claimed finite instance does not match the picture. Each X_i must have m bits by §2. Figure 2 says m=4 but draws eight bits in each X_i; its TeX loops over 1,...,8 and even puts zeros at positions 7 and 5. This is a dimension error in the illustration, not a failure of the coupling argument.
entry.why_it_matters: A reader checking the displayed example cannot instantiate the paper’s own definition with the shown parameters.
entry.advice: Draw four-bit X_i strings with row positions in [4], or explicitly make the picture a schematic with omitted dimensions. A labelled m=4 instance should literally satisfy its stated sizes.

locator.quote: the address inputs, drawn from $\mu$, are the same in both.

entry.feedback: The caption correctly says the address blocks are shared, but the picture gives each panel separate boxes labelled by the sampling law. Visually, those can be read as two independent samplings from the same distribution.
entry.why_it_matters: Equality of the sampled address data is the coupling, while equality in distribution is insufficient for the first-difference argument.
entry.advice: Give corresponding address blocks the same identifiers or a visible “unchanged” cue. Preserve the caption’s explicit statement of shared data.

locator.quote: puts a single zero at $X_i[J_i]$, draws every $A_{i,h}$ from $\mu$, all mutually independent,

entry.feedback: One sentence generates the rows, writes the matrix, samples the address instances, declares independence and fills every cell. The phrase “all mutually independent” has to be read backwards across two sampling operations and an intervening deterministic assignment.
entry.why_it_matters: The distribution is central enough that its random choices should be immediately identifiable.
entry.advice: Separate the two random sampling choices from the deterministic assignments, and state their joint independence beside the choices. A short prose sequence or a compact definition display would work.

locator.quote: since $J_i$ is uniform on the unqueried rows

entry.feedback: This conditional uniformity holds while the zero in column i has not yet been discovered. After it has been found, J_i is known; a repeated query to that row returns zero with probability one. The intended count is of first discoveries, but the preceding sentence says “a query ... finds the zero” without explicitly restricting to undiscovered columns.
entry.why_it_matters: The stated hazard estimate is too broad if read literally, although the first-discovery argument gives the intended bound.
entry.advice: Say that the early-discovery estimate concerns a previously undiscovered zero, and that repeated queries make no new discovery. Keep the count of distinct queried rows separate from the total query budget.

locator.quote: A sharper count, which we cite from

entry.feedback: The optional sentence gives 2G/(m(m+1)) without naming which of the two quantities in the preceding display it bounds. Its last clause then says the improvement is unused.
entry.why_it_matters: A minor refinement creates both a referent question and an interruption after the essential estimate has been proved.
entry.advice: Omit it from the short paper, or explicitly identify it as the erased-zero hit probability and place it in a brief optional remark.

locator.quote: We turn this into a predictor for the answers of one column.

entry.feedback: This paragraph contains the observation about query positions, the fixed i and time tau, the free data, the simulation rule, the abort, the output convention, the cap implication and the event inclusion. All of these steps matter, but the 164-word paragraph makes the reduction harder to audit than the reduction itself.
entry.why_it_matters: The reader needs to distinguish construction of the predictor from the implication connecting it to the original run.
entry.advice: End a first paragraph after the predictor’s output rule, then state its cap and the event inclusion together. Preserve the exact order: output address is named before reading cell contents.

locator.quote: it aborts before an $(L+1)$-st query to them in total.

entry.feedback: Lemma 4 concerns a vector-output algorithm. The word “aborts” can instead suggest an algorithm with a separate failure symbol, while the fixed-vector convention is described only in the following if/otherwise sentence.
entry.why_it_matters: The total-output convention matters when applying the direct-product bound to every branch of the constructed predictor.
entry.advice: State explicitly that an aborted simulation returns the fixed vector. This is only a clarification of the reduction already described.

locator.quote: This bounds a joint event under the original law.

entry.feedback: This sentence gives exactly the probabilistic interpretation of (12). It prevents the common but invalid step of applying the direct product after conditioning on a query-budget event that depends on the hard inputs.
entry.why_it_matters: The lower bound’s adaptive simulation is credible because the original law and the capped predictor remain visible.
entry.advice: Retain the sentence, the conditional-versus-joint distinction and the concrete counterexample destination.

locator.quote: Summing (12) over the $G$ times, averaging over the independent $I$

entry.feedback: The final G beta^r term is correct, but the disappearance of a potential factor m is hidden in the phrase “averaging”. The preceding bound was established for each fixed column, so this is a natural place for a reader to pause.
entry.why_it_matters: The product of the unknown-column factor and the query-time union bound is the quantitative heart of this argument.
entry.advice: Show or state the intermediate (1/m) sum over i followed by the sum over tau. The m terms cancel against the averaging factor; no stronger result is needed.

locator.quote: whereas error at most $1/3$ on the zero-input $Y^{(0)}$ and the one-input $Y^{(1)}$

entry.feedback: Y^(0) and Y^(1) are random inputs, but this sentence talks about each as a single input. The intended implication is that worst-case correctness holds at every point of each support, and hence also after averaging.
entry.why_it_matters: The reader should be able to see the move from a worst-case algorithm to a distributional acceptance gap without translating the terminology.
entry.advice: Say that the algorithm is correct on every input in the two supports, or explicitly mention averaging the pointwise error guarantees.

locator.quote: For the constant in (2), take $k\ge2$, $t\ge8$

entry.feedback: The lower-bound proof reaches its conceptual conclusion at (15), then ends with a full floor-removal calculation and two record pointers. The exact constant is useful as a checkable output, but this routine calculation is not what the expert needs to remember from the section.
entry.why_it_matters: The proof finishes on arithmetic rather than on the mechanism that supplied mL.
entry.advice: Keep the explicit resulting constant and threshold, and move the intermediate inequalities to a short note or the record. A single well-targeted link is enough.

locator.quote: Theorem 1 uses only (5).

entry.feedback: The first paragraph repeats the Bansal–Sinha formula already given after property (i), then restates why it implies (5) for fixed k. The repetition is not needed to introduce the different uniform estimate.
entry.why_it_matters: The section spends its opening re-establishing a dependency that the reader already accepted.
entry.advice: Refer back to the cited fixed-k hardness statement and use the saved space to say what new control the uniform estimate supplies.

locator.quote: by a stopped-martingale induction in the style of Girish, Tal and Wu

entry.feedback: The outline names a rounded Gaussian chain, a multilinear extension, derivatives, a stopped martingale, an amplified tree of depth 50kD+1 and a gap of order 18^{-(k-1)} in one paragraph. It is neither a usable sketch of the proof nor a simple explanation of its role. The numerical losses are introduced before the reason for them.
entry.why_it_matters: An expert outside this particular lower-bound method receives a chain of technique names rather than an explanation to carry to the record.
entry.advice: First explain the two competing estimates on the same acceptance gap and why off-promise mass forces error reduction. Then give the record route. Leave the numerical amplification constants with the detailed proof.

locator.quote: The constants in (16) are the record's.

entry.feedback: The record is treated as an actor, and the sentence does not say whether it contributes a new estimate, explicit evaluation of existing constants, or a reconstruction of published arguments. The preceding sentence contains the mathematical distinction, while this short sentence adds document bookkeeping.
entry.why_it_matters: It foregrounds where material lives rather than what was proved and how it relates to the cited literature.
entry.advice: Attach the source and scope directly to the bound or its derivation. Keep the substantive comparison of k- and logarithmic dependence; remove the document-as-author phrasing.

locator.quote: so it is not the minimax law $\mu$ of §4

entry.feedback: The text correctly distinguishes the law used to prove Forrelation hardness from the promised-input law subsequently obtained by minimax. This is especially useful because both arguments use planting language.
entry.why_it_matters: The distinction prevents an invalid import of off-promise mass into the direct-product lower bound.
entry.advice: Keep the local explanation of the two laws. It is mathematical orientation, not dispensable evidence bureaucracy.
entry.round6_context: Round-six CX021 and CX048 are visibly addressed.

locator.quote: Keep $k$ fixed and let $m=4^t$ grow.

entry.feedback: The proof chooses an exponent to exclude, then one fixed k, and only then sends m to infinity. The displayed ratio makes the strict exponent gap absorb every fixed polylogarithmic factor.
entry.why_it_matters: This is the exact inference needed for the infimum in (1), and it can be checked without reading the growing-k refinement.
entry.advice: Keep the ratio argument and the order of choices. Do not replace it with an informal substitution of a growing k into fixed-k bounds.

locator.quote: The exponent tends to four, and the family still gives no bound $R=\Omega(Q^4)$.

entry.feedback: The immediately preceding fixed-k paragraph already says the result does not give R=Omega(Q^4). Repeating the caveat at the end of the growing-k remark makes the section close twice on the same limitation.
entry.why_it_matters: The distinction is important, but repeated defensive endings weaken the conclusion.
entry.advice: State the endpoint distinction once after both forms of the result, while preserving the different quantifier regimes.

locator.quote: With $k=\lfloor\sqrt{t/20}\rfloor$ and $t\ge80$

entry.feedback: The remark contains a second choice of L, the explicit exponential quantum constant, a schedule, a long epsilon formula and the resulting family notation. Its derivation has correctly moved to the record, but its statement still reads like a compressed second theorem embedded in one paragraph.
entry.why_it_matters: The main exponent proof is complete; the reader now has to parse a separate quantitative regime to reach the formalisation section.
entry.advice: Retain the reason uniformity is needed, the schedule if it helps, and the asymptotic conclusion. Put the detailed epsilon expression and parameter bookkeeping with the linked derivation.
entry.round6_context: Round-six C10-growing-k supplied the missing derivation in the record. This finding concerns the remaining density of the short remark, not a missing proof.

locator.quote: ## 7. The formal statement

entry.feedback: The previous apparatus has been removed, which is an improvement, but the formal section still occupies more than a printed page in five dense paragraphs. It covers four endpoints, the models, empty infima, two universal-upper-bound constants, existential parameters, two amplifier forms and a recursive cap event.
entry.why_it_matters: The expert paper’s ending is dominated by correspondence detail even though the long record already has a dedicated formal-evidence appendix.
entry.advice: Keep a short mathematical account of the headline formal theorem and the distinctions that materially change its reading. Route the auxiliary-lemma comparison and secondary constants to the record with readable links.
entry.round6_context: Round-six C02-appendix-size was addressed by relocation and removal of receipts. The revised section remains overweight; do not restore hashes, commands or review-status ledgers.

locator.quote: The four statements carry no hypotheses, so their proofs are complete;

entry.feedback: The inference expressed by “so” is too compressed. A statement’s lack of hypotheses alone does not establish proof completeness. Here the preceding account of separately checked proofs and allowed axioms is doing that work, and the following paragraphs still discuss how the formal definitions relate to the printed mathematics.
entry.why_it_matters: The sentence can sound like a blanket assurance precisely where a conventional, scoped mathematical description would be clearer.
entry.advice: Describe the four formal endpoints as unconditional in their stated definitions and let the preceding proof-checking sentence carry the verification fact. Do not add a review-status disclaimer.

locator.quote: The definitions follow §1.

entry.feedback: This paragraph repeats the oracle-only access, worst-case cap and two-thirds success conventions from the opening. Its new information is the finite-mixture and deferred-measurement bridges, but the repeated material comes first.
entry.why_it_matters: The reader must scan familiar definitions to locate the actual reason the formal model corresponds to the usual one.
entry.advice: Refer back to §1 for the conventions, then give only the mathematical content and destinations of the two bridges. Preserve their separate links.

locator.quote: A second Lean proof follows OpenAI's Appendix A

entry.feedback: The formal section introduces 20736 and then 35^4 for two proofs of the same universal exponent. Neither numerical constant is used in the argument of this companion; alpha_tot only needs the existence of a universal constant.
entry.why_it_matters: The final section invites comparison of auxiliary constants that does not help the reader assess the main theorem or the correspondence of its models.
entry.advice: Keep the formal universal quartic bound and credit to its route. Move the alternative proof and numerical comparison to the record, where they can be inspected without competing with the main statement.

locator.quote: Its logarithmic exponent $b$ is existential, and its lower bound is the floor form (15)

entry.feedback: This plainly identifies a real difference between the main formal endpoint and the explicit printed bound, then names the separate theorem supplying the constants. It is the right level of mathematical correspondence for an expert paper.
entry.why_it_matters: A reader can understand what the headline formal theorem says without reading Lean syntax.
